citations.quote: Assume countable choice as required by the chosen tubular-neighborhood and peripheral-system data. Let K be a smooth oriented knot with compact exterior E_K, positive meridian mu_K, and preferred longitude lambda_K on the boundary torus. The zero-framed surgery manifold M(K) is the closed oriented 3-manifold obtained by gluing D²×S¹ to E_K so that the meridian boundary circle of D²×{1} is identified with lambda_K and the core {0}×S¹ is identified with mu_K. The orientation extends the orientation of E_K across the filling. Thus the filling slope is the preferred zero-linking longitude; the definition asserts no 4-manifold bounded by M(K).

Let $X$ be a four-dimensional manifold with boundary and let $W$ be a compact surface with boundary. An embedding $e:(W,\partial W)\to(X,\partial X)$ is proper when $e^{-1}(\partial X)=\partial W$. It is locally flat at an interior point of $W$ when there are neighborhoods of the point and its image and a homeomorphism of pairs from those neighborhoods to $(\mathbb R^4,\mathbb R^2)$, with the standard linear plane $\mathbb R^2\subset\mathbb R^4$. It is locally flat at a boundary point when there are such neighborhoods and a homeomorphism of pairs to $(\mathbb R^4_+,\mathbb R^2_+)$, where $\mathbb R^4_+=\{x_4\geq0\}$ and $\mathbb R^2_+=\{x_2=x_3=0,\ x_4\geq0\}$; the line $\partial\mathbb R^2_+$ lies in $\partial\mathbb R^4_+$. A collar of a boundary circle of $W$ is an embedding of that circle times $[0,\varepsilon)$ into $W$ that is the identity on the circle at parameter $0$; a concordance collar is required to agree with the corresponding product collar of the ambient end. A smooth proper surface has the analogous smooth charts and collars, which are also topological locally flat charts.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

derivations.claim: Put $E=\overline{W\setminus N}$, $C=A\times S^1$, and $E_i=E\cap S_i^3$, $N_i=N\cap S_i^3$, $C_i=C\cap S_i^3$. The supplied product identifies $N$ with $S^1\times I\times D^2$, $N_i$ with $S^1\times\{i\}\times D^2$, $C$ with $S^1\times I\times S^1$, and $C_i$ with its endpoint torus. Attach $F=D^2\times S^1\times I$ along $C$, identifying its disk-boundary circle with the annulus longitude and its other circle with the normal meridian. Each endpoint boundary is then $E_i$ filled by $F_i=D^2\times S^1\times\{i\}$ along the preferred longitude, precisely $M(K_i)$ by [F1]. The common annular-side collar gives a manifold after gluing, with the same smooth or topological category as the supplied data; in the smooth case round the product corners. This constructs $V=E\cup_C F$ with the prescribed oriented ends.

Here is the relative chain comparison in every degree. Thicken the pieces slightly along their supplied common collars to make excisive covers, using the same thickening at the ends; the thickenings retract onto the indicated pieces and intersections as pairs. For either decomposition $X=P\cup_C Q$ with corresponding endpoint $X_i=P_i\cup_{C_i}Q_i$, the small-chain sequence underlying [F3], quotiented by the endpoint sequence, is degreewise exact: $0\to C_*(C,C_i;R)\to C_*(P,P_i;R)\oplus C_*(Q,Q_i;R)\to C_*^{\mathrm{small}}(X,X_i;R)\to0$, with maps $c\mapsto(c,-c)$ and $(p,q)\mapsto p+q$. Exactness follows simplex by simplex, and subdivision and its prism preserve the endpoint chains, so the last complex computes $H_*(X,X_i;R)$. Its connecting map sends a relative cycle $p+q$ to the class of $\partial p=-\partial q$ in the intersection quotient. Thus it supplies the relative exact sequence in all degrees, including degrees zero and one, rather than only a comparison of absolute ranks.

The endpoint inclusions $N_i\to N$ and $C_i\to C$ are deformation retractions up to inverse inclusion, by linearly contracting the $I$ coordinate to $i$. Their relative homology groups therefore vanish in every degree. Apply step 2.1 to $(W,S_i^3)=(E,E_i)\cup(N,N_i)$: the exact sequence gives $H_k(E,E_i;R)\cong H_k(W,S_i^3;R)$ for every $k$. The latter groups vanish because $S_i^3\to W$ induces homology isomorphisms in every degree, as follows directly from the long exact sequence of this pair. Next $F_i\to F$ is also a product deformation retraction. Applying the same exact sequence to $(V,M(K_i))=(E,E_i)\cup(F,F_i)$ gives $H_k(V,M(K_i);R)\cong H_k(E,E_i;R)=0$ for every $k$. The pair sequence now proves that each $M(K_i)\to V$ is an $R$-homology isomorphism, including in degree zero and the top degrees.

Suppose finally that $\pi_1(W)=1$. The exterior $E$ is connected: $W$ is connected, $N$ and its side $C$ are connected, and any other component of the manifold $E$ would be a component of $W$ disjoint from the gluing side. Choose basepoint paths in $C$ and write $\ell,m$ for its annulus and meridian circles. The map $\pi_1(C)\to\pi_1(N)$ is surjective with kernel normally generated by $m$. The pushout [F4] consequently identifies $\pi_1(W)$ with $\pi_1(E)/\langle\!\langle m\rangle\!\rangle$; this follows also directly by eliminating the generator $\ell$ of the second factor in its amalgamated presentation. Thus $m$ normally generates $\pi_1(E)$. For the second gluing, $\pi_1(C)\to\pi_1(F)$ is surjective with kernel generated by $\ell$, so the same elimination gives $\pi_1(V)=\pi_1(E)/\langle\!\langle\ell\rangle\!\rangle$. The image of $m$ still normally generates this quotient and lies in each endpoint knot-exterior group, hence in its zero-surgery group image. This proves the stated endpoint normal-generation conclusion. The proof uses the normal neighborhood already assumed in the Statement and makes no assertion that local flatness alone constructs it.

citations.quote: Let knots be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented S³ and let I=[0,1]. Let C_sm be their smooth concordance classes, where equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in S³×I. Let C_top be their locally flat topological concordance classes in that product. Let C_ex be their exotic-smooth concordance classes: equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W together with an orientation-preserving homeomorphism of pairs (W,∂W)≅(S³×I,S³×{0,1}) matching the endpoint knots. The annulus is oriented so that its boundary is −K₀ at the lower end and K₁ at the upper end, and it has product collars at both ends agreeing with the ambient boundary collars. For a nonzero integer n set R_n=Z[1/|n|]. Let C^{1/n} be the classes under equivalence witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W with boundary the two standard endpoint 3-spheres such that each boundary inclusion induces an isomorphism H_i(S³;R_n)→H_i(W;R_n) for every i. The annulus is oriented so that its boundary is −K₀ at the lower end and K₁ at the upper end, with product collars at both ends agreeing with the ambient boundary collars. A knot is pseudo-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold homeomorphic to B⁴, with its oriented boundary identified with the standard oriented S³. A knot is Z[1/|n|]-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold B with its oriented boundary identified with the standard oriented S³ and with H_i(B;R_n)≅H_i(B⁴;R_n) for every i; such a B is an R_n-homology 4-ball. These are sets of equivalence classes; this definition alone asserts no group structure.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, let $B^4=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\lVert x\rVert^2\le1\}$ with boundary $S^3$. The oriented connected sum $K\#K^\dagger$ bounds a smooth properly embedded disk $D\subset B^4$ for which the squared radial function $\rho(x)=\lVert x\rVert^2$ restricts to a Morse function on the interior of $D$ with all critical points of index $0$ or $1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. On oriented ambient-isotopy classes of smooth knots in $S^3$, the connected-sum operation is associative and commutative, and the standard unknot is a two-sided identity. Here “commutative monoid” means a set with an associative binary operation, a two-sided identity, and equality after interchanging the two inputs.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Specialize the TOP/exotic external assertion [F5] at each finite list of knot representatives and witnessing annuli actually used. For TOP these lie in the standard product; for exotic concordance the supplied boundary-marked homeomorphism to that product is part of the input code. The finite chart and pair-chart extraction in [F6] uses compactness, not a choice of an atlas for a countable family. Inside $L[r]$ use the ordinary CDR group operation, retain the actual output annulus and marked product homeomorphism, and export their compact forward/inverse and collar certificates. This proves the required finite compatibility and transitivity instances in $V$. Since each instance starts with its own given finite data, no simultaneous choice of representatives or witnesses for all classes is made. The quotient group operations and laws follow by universal quantification over these instances; the original $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypothesis is therefore respected, rather than inferred from the unqualified source assertion. The localized category is handled directly by the subsequent homology calculations, with no TOP normal theorem needed.

Let $D\subset B^4$ be the smooth ribbon disk for $K\#K^\dagger$ supplied by [F2]. By local smooth coordinates and straightening of the embedded disk, choose an ambiently standard interior 4-ball $B$ such that $B\cap D$ is a standard 2-disk. An ambient isotopy supported in the interior carries $B$ to a concentric standard ball, so its complement in $B^4$ is diffeomorphic to $S^3\times I$. Removing $\operatorname{int}B$ from $B^4$ and the interior of $B\cap D$ from $D$ gives a smooth annulus. The outer and inner boundary collars give product collars for it. Order the ends with $K\#K^\dagger$ at the lower end and the inner standard unknot at the upper end, and orient the annulus so its boundary is $-(K\#K^\dagger)$ at the lower end and $U$ at the upper end. It is therefore an admissible inverse concordance in the smooth category, and the same product annulus satisfies the TOP, exotic and localized ambient conditions.

The supplied connected-sum theorem gives associativity, commutativity and the unknot identity at the level of oriented knot types. The retained standard smooth boundary-sum construction on witnessing annuli gives concordance compatibility in the standard smooth product; the TOP/exotic compatibility is the external input [F5], and the localized ambient verification is given by the subsequent homology calculations. The knot-type isotopies themselves are admissible annuli in every category.

The external input [F5] supplies the TOP and exotic ambient gluing/compatibility assertions at exactly the definitions in [F1]. For the localized smooth category, transitivity is stacking along the marked $S^3$: Mayer–Vietoris and the two boundary homology isomorphisms give another $R_n$-homology $S^3\times I$. Reflection gives symmetry and a product gives reflexivity, all with their smooth annulus collars.

For localized connected sum choose a smooth product neighborhood $D^3\times I$ of a proper spanning arc inside each witnessing annulus, with the annulus strip in its standard local position, and remove its interior. If $Q$ is the remaining ambient piece, excision gives $H_j(W,Q;R_n)=R_n$ only for $j=3$. The map $H_3(W;R_n)\to H_3(W,Q;R_n)$ is an isomorphism: the boundary fundamental class meets the spanning arc once. The pair sequence therefore makes $Q$ an $R_n$-homology ball. Glue the two such complements on $S^2\times I$, joining the annulus strips. Mayer–Vietoris gives $R_n$ in degrees0 and3 and zero in other positive degrees; the endpoint connected-sum spheres give the degree3 generator, so each end inclusion is a homology isomorphism. Let V=S¹×D² be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core, meridional disk and product longitude. A pattern is a smooth oriented knot P in the interior of V. Its winding number w(P) is its algebraic intersection with an oriented meridional disk, equivalently the coefficient of the core in [P]∈H₁(V;Z). For a smooth oriented knot K in S³, let e_K:V→S³ be a zero-framed tubular embedding carrying the core to K and carrying the meridian and product longitude to the positive meridian and preferred longitude of K. The satellite knot P(K) is e_K(P).

When concordance preservation has been established, the formula [K]↦[P(K)] defines a set map on each of C_sm, C_top, C_ex and C^{1/n}. The solid-torus meridian is strong winding number ±1 for P if, after V is embedded as the standard unknotted solid torus and P(U) denotes the resulting closure, that meridian normally generates π₁(S³\P(U)). Normal generation means that the smallest normal subgroup containing the element is the whole group. Strong winding number ±1 is a separate condition from ordinary winding number ±1. No additivity or homomorphism property is part of this definition.

Let $V=S^1\times D^2$ be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core $S^1\times\{0\}$. A **pattern** is a smooth oriented knot $P$ contained in the interior of $V$, together with a chosen closed tubular neighbourhood $N(P)$ contained in the interior of $V$. Its **winding number** $w(P)$ is the integer by which the homology class $[P]$ maps to $H_1(V;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ under the isomorphism that sends the oriented core to $1$. The **pattern exterior** is $X_P=V\setminus\operatorname{int}N(P)$; its **outer torus** is $\partial V$ and its **inner torus** is $\partial N(P)$. A **companion** is a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ with a specified orientation-preserving tubular embedding $e:V\to S^3$ that sends the core to $K$ and identifies the solid-torus meridian and product longitude with the positive meridian and preferred longitude of $K$. The **satellite knot** $P(K)$ is $e(P)$, with chosen exterior $E_{P(K)}=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}e(N(P))$; the image $e(\partial V)$ is its **companion torus**. The outer torus is **incompressible** when it bounds no properly embedded disk in $X_P$ with essential boundary on $\partial V$. It is **product-parallel** to the inner torus when $X_P$ is a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with those tori as its ends. This definition alone asserts neither incompressibility nor essentiality of the companion torus.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

derivations.claim: A transverse meridional disk exists for every smooth pattern, without a selection axiom. Parametrize $P$ by its supplied circle embedding and compose with the angular projection of the solid torus to obtain a smooth circle map $f$. Its angular derivative is a continuous real function on the parameter circle. For $0<\delta<1/2$, uniform continuity allows a partition into finitely many equal short intervals such that on any interval meeting the zero set of $f'$ one has $|f'|<\delta$. Make the intervals short enough to lift the map to real angular coordinates there. The images of these intervals have total arc length at most $\delta$, by integrating this derivative bound over intervals of total length at most one. Those finitely many image arcs cannot cover the target circle of length one: cutting at their finitely many endpoints and adding the lengths proves this finite covering inequality directly. Choose an angle outside them. Every preimage is regular, so its meridional disk is transverse; the case of empty preimage is allowed. Only one angle and finitely many intervals are selected. The specified transverse disk in the Statement may be any such disk.

Represent $K\#J$ by concatenating long representatives of $K$ and $J$, each constant in its endpoint product collars, and then closing by the fixed trivial outside arc. Use their zero-framed tubular products, glued by the identity on the two normal disk coordinates. This is the zero-framed product of the connected sum: a longitude and the core have linking zero on each of the two separated summand portions, their connecting parallel arcs are untwisted, and cross linking vanishes because those portions lie in disjoint balls. Their total linking is therefore zero. This checks the framing rather than introducing an unspecified meridional twist at the concatenation.

Let the disk meet $P$ in the finite transverse set $p_1,\ldots,p_m$. Finiteness follows because this inverse image is a compact discrete subset of the compact knot. Shrink the slab so that its intersection with $P$ consists of exactly $m$ arcs crossing from one disk face to the other. Indeed transversality gives each intersection a local graph over the slab coordinate; finitely many disjoint such neighborhoods suffice, and the compact remaining part of $P$ is disjoint from the central disk and hence from a sufficiently short slab. Straighten the graph arcs in disjoint small disks about the $p_j$. Explicitly, if the $j$th graph has disk coordinate $p_j(t)$, use $(q,t)\mapsto(q+\chi_j(q)(p_j(0)-p_j(t)),t)$, with $\chi_j=1$ near that graph and zero outside its disk. Work first in a slightly larger slab and multiply the displacement by a smooth time-coordinate cutoff $\tau(t)$ equal to one on the inner slab and zero near the larger slab faces. Thus the isotopy is the identity at the outside faces and glues to the identity off the larger slab. After shortening the slab its derivative in $q$ differs from the identity by norm less than $1/2$; the straight-line interpolation has the same bound and is an isotopy. Each disk map is a diffeomorphism: solve its inverse by the uniformly contracting iteration $q_{k+1}=z-\tau(t)\chi_j(q_k)(p_j(0)-p_j(t))$, and use [F3] at its everywhere invertible derivative to obtain smooth local inverses, which agree with this unique inverse. Thus the pattern can be represented as one remaining tangle joined to $m$ straight parallel strands across the chosen slab, with some of their orientations possibly reversed.

Cut a small standard arc from $K$, leaving a long knot in a product ball whose two end neighborhoods are straight. Its zero-framed normal product yields $m$ disjoint parallel copies, one for each supplied point $p_j$ after a disk-coordinate rescaling. The product is constant at the ends and its framing has no full twist. Insert this whole string link in the straight-strand slab and retain the other tangle from step 2.1. All endpoint coordinates agree, so the result is a smooth embedded oriented knot in the original solid torus, denoted $P_K$. Negative-oriented strands follow the same geometric parallel copy with the opposite orientation; they are not omitted or replaced by a differently framed tangle.

Insert the tangle description of $P$ from step 2.1 into the product of step 1.2. Across the long $K$ portion it has exactly the $m$ parallel strands constructed in step 3.1. Across the long $J$ portion it has the corresponding parallel strands of $J$, and the remainder is the unchanged tangle of $P$. One may now absorb the $K$ portion into that remainder, leaving $J$ as the sole companion portion. The resulting tangle is precisely $P_K$ inserted into the zero-framed neighborhood of $J$. The disk products agree on every common face, so these are the same glued oriented embedding after the chosen product reparametrizations; smoothing the matching straight collars gives an oriented isotopy. Hence $P(K\#J)$ is isotopic to $P_K(J)$. No step replaces all $m$ strands by a local knot in one strand.

Both the original straight $m$-strand tangle and its replacement lie in a product ball inside a slightly smaller meridional-disk slab containing all $p_j$, and they agree on its boundary. Their oriented difference is a one-cycle in that ball, hence bounds there (contract the ball linearly). They therefore represent the same class in the homology of the solid torus. Their algebraic coefficient of its core, namely the winding number, is unchanged. This proves the second conclusion as well, including winding zero and mixed strand orientations.

derivations.claim: For the TOP annulus the ambient manifold is the standard compact product, and the given annulus and end collars have exactly the finite pair-code description in [F5]. Apply the external normal theorem [F3] inside $L[r]$ with those collars. Restrict the resulting tube to a compact disk bundle, still with a slightly wider domain, and export its forward/inverse, pair and collar certificates as in [F5]. This gives an actual relative tube in $V$ without ambient AC. For the smooth annuli in the other three categories, a finite chart partition of unity gives a metric and connection along the compact annulus; parallel transport and the compact inverse-function construction give the smooth tube. Only finitely many chart choices and least integer radii are needed. Thus the external TOP input used below is earned at this particular finite input; no global choice-free version of FQ is being asserted.

In the smooth product category, choose a tubular neighborhood of the smooth annulus A. Its oriented normal 2-plane bundle over A has relative Euler obstruction in H²(A,∂A;Z)≅Z. The boundary trivializations are the zero framings of K₀ and K₁; the relative obstruction is the difference of their self-linking numbers, hence zero. A relative framing therefore identifies a neighborhood of A with A×D² and agrees with the two prescribed endpoint zero-framed neighborhoods.

In that framed neighborhood insert $P$ in every disk fiber. Orient the inserted annulus by the interval direction followed by the pattern orientation. Its oriented boundary is then $-P(K_0)$ at the lower end and $P(K_1)$ at the upper end. The product collars of $A$ and the endpoint framings give product collars matching the ambient end collars, and the two endpoint patterns use the preferred zero framings. This proves concordance preservation for smooth annuli in a standard product.

In the exotic and localized cases the annulus is smooth, so the same smooth tubular construction is available in its given smooth ambient manifold. In the TOP case use the external input [F3] relative to the two actual smooth endpoint collars. In every case this gives an oriented rank-two vector normal bundle over $A$. Its obstruction to a framing extending the two preferred zero framings is its relative Euler number in $H^2(A,\partial A;\mathbb Z)$. Cap $A$ by boundary Seifert chains with opposite boundary orientations and push the caps into the product collars. Their union is a closed two-cycle. Its intersection with a relative small parallel copy of $A$ is the relative Euler number, because the two cap terms are precisely the endpoint zero-linking numbers. The cycle is zero over $R$ by [F4], so that Euler number is zero in $R$. The inclusion $\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow R$ is injective, hence it is zero integrally. Classification of oriented plane bundles with boundary framing now gives a framing of the actual normal bundle agreeing with both preferred endpoint framings. This proves the required relative framing, rather than inferring it from absolute triviality.

Insert the product annulus $P\times I$ into this framed neighborhood, as in step1.2. Its endpoint knots are the untwisted satellites because both endpoint framings are the preferred zero framings. In the TOP case the product model makes the new annulus locally flat; in the three smooth categories it is smooth. The ambient manifold is the original $W$, so its homeomorphism or $R$-homology conditions do not change. Thus the satellite assignment preserves concordance in all four categories and descends to the stated set maps.

Its winding number w(P) is its algebraic intersection with an oriented meridional disk, equivalently the coefficient of the core in [P]∈H₁(V;Z). For a smooth oriented knot K in S³, let e_K:V→S³ be a zero-framed tubular embedding carrying the core to K and carrying the meridian and product longitude to the positive meridian and preferred longitude of K. The satellite knot P(K) is e_K(P).

When concordance preservation has been established, the formula [K]↦[P(K)] defines a set map on each of C_sm, C_top, C_ex and C^{1/n}. The solid-torus meridian is strong winding number ±1 for P if, after V is embedded as the standard unknotted solid torus and P(U) denotes the resulting closure, that meridian normally generates π₁(S³\P(U)). Normal generation means that the smallest normal subgroup containing the element is the whole group. Strong winding number ±1 is a separate condition from ordinary winding number ±1. No additivity or homomorphism property is part of this definition.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

derivations.claim: Let λ denote the longitude of the pattern solid torus. Filling the outer boundary of the pattern exterior along λ produces S³∖P(U), so the induced epimorphism π₁(ST∖P)→π₁(S³∖P(U)) has kernel normally generated by λ. By [F1], the target is normally generated by the image of η; hence π₁(ST∖P) is normally generated by η and λ.

For a local connected sum with any knot J, the closure-complement group is the amalgamated product of the two knot groups along their common meridian, by cutting at the connected-sum sphere and applying van Kampen. Each knot-group factor is normally generated by its meridian.

Decompose the complement of P(K) along the companion torus into ST∖P and S³∖K. Van Kampen gives a generating set normally contained in the images of these two groups. The first is normally generated by η and λ by step 1.1; the second is normally generated by μ_K by [F3].

Under the torus gluing, λ is identified with λ_K and η with μ_K. Since μ_K normally generates the companion-knot group, λ becomes redundant, and η normally generates the entire satellite-complement group. The outer solid-torus meridian for the pattern P(K) is isotopic in the complement to η, so it too normally generates.

The solid-torus meridian normally generates the strong-winding factor by hypothesis; quotienting the amalgamated product by that meridian kills this factor and the common meridian. The other knot-group factor is then killed because its meridian normally generates it. Thus the whole closure-complement group is normally generated by the solid-torus meridian.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice as required by the chosen tubular-neighborhood and peripheral-system data. Let K be a smooth oriented knot with compact exterior E_K, positive meridian mu_K, and preferred longitude lambda_K on the boundary torus. The zero-framed surgery manifold M(K) is the closed oriented 3-manifold obtained by gluing D²×S¹ to E_K so that the meridian boundary circle of D²×{1} is identified with lambda_K and the core {0}×S¹ is identified with mu_K. The orientation extends the orientation of E_K across the filling. Thus the filling slope is the preferred zero-linking longitude; the definition asserts no 4-manifold bounded by M(K).

Let V=S¹×D² be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core, meridional disk and product longitude. A pattern is a smooth oriented knot P in the interior of V. Its winding number w(P) is its algebraic intersection with an oriented meridional disk, equivalently the coefficient of the core in [P]∈H₁(V;Z). For a smooth oriented knot K in S³, let e_K:V→S³ be a zero-framed tubular embedding carrying the core to K and carrying the meridian and product longitude to the positive meridian and preferred longitude of K. The satellite knot P(K) is e_K(P).

When concordance preservation has been established, the formula [K]↦[P(K)] defines a set map on each of C_sm, C_top, C_ex and C^{1/n}. The solid-torus meridian is strong winding number ±1 for P if, after V is embedded as the standard unknotted solid torus and P(U) denotes the resulting closure, that meridian normally generates π₁(S³\P(U)). Normal generation means that the smallest normal subgroup containing the element is the whole group. Strong winding number ±1 is a separate condition from ordinary winding number ±1. No additivity or homomorphism property is part of this definition.

Let $P\cup\eta$ be a smooth oriented two-component link in $S^3$ with unknotted axis $\eta$, and let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot. Supply disjoint closed product tubes and positive meridian/preferred zero-linking-longitude peripheral data for the knots and axis. Write $P(K)$ for infection along $\eta$ with the untwisted companion $K$. For a knot $L$, write $M(L)$ for its actual chosen zero-longitude filling, with the orientation extending its exterior. Let $w=\operatorname{lk}(P,\eta)$.

There is a compact oriented smooth cobordism $E$ with
$$\partial E=M(P)\sqcup M(K)\sqcup(-M(P(K))).$$
For any commutative unital coefficient ring $R$, it has $H_1(E;R)=R$ and $H_2(E;R)=R^2$. The two first boundary components induce the displayed basis in degree two. If $s_L=\alpha_L\cap[M(L)]$ where $\alpha_L\in H^1(M(L);R)$ evaluates as $1$ on the positive meridian, then, in those coordinates,
$$i_*s_{P(K)}=i_*s_P+w\,i_*s_K.$$
In degree one the meridians of $P$, $K$ and $P(K)$ map to $1,w,1$, respectively.

Likewise, for any finite nonempty list of knots $K_1,\ldots,K_q$ with the same supplied peripheral data, there is a compact oriented smooth cobordism $C$ from $\bigsqcup_j M(K_j)$ to $M(K_1\#\cdots\#K_q)$, with $H_1(C;R)=R$ and $H_2(C;R)=R^q$. The incoming degree-two classes are its coordinate basis and the outgoing class maps to their sum. In particular, for $X=E$ or $C$, the outgoing inclusions are injective on $H_1,H_2$ and the union of incoming components surjects onto $H_2(X;R)$.

The peripheral and framing data are supplied, rather than selected by an existence theorem. Their subsequent construction and the homology assertions use no additional choice principle. This is an ordinary-coefficient assertion; arbitrary twisted-coefficient boundary generation is not asserted.

Let $E$ be the actual standard infection cobordism from $M(P)\sqcup M(K)$ to $M(P(K))$, constructed from the two surgery products by identifying $N(\eta)$ with the filling solid torus $V_K$. Supply the oriented product tubes and peripheral paths, with $\mu_\eta=\lambda_K$ and $\lambda_\eta=\mu_K$ on the common torus, where $\lambda_K$ is the companion's preferred longitude. No winding-number condition is needed. The inclusion-induced homomorphism is onto and induces
$$\pi_1(M(P(K)))/\langle\!\langle\lambda_K\rangle\!\rangle\ \cong\ \pi_1(E).$$
The marked companion meridian and pattern-axis core have the same image in $\pi_1(E)$, with the supplied base paths.

More generally, if a connected manifold $W$ with supplied boundary collar is glued to $E$ along the marked outgoing component $M(P(K))$, the inclusion-induced map is onto and gives
$$\pi_1(W)/\langle\!\langle i_*(\lambda_K)\rangle\!\rangle\ \cong\ \pi_1(W\cup_{M(P(K))}E).$$
Changing a peripheral base path changes the relator by conjugation and leaves its normal closure unchanged. The statements hold for topological collared $W$ as well as smooth $W$ and use no choice axiom.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

derivations.claim: The smooth disk tube uses [F5] directly. In the TOP branch the input is a single locally flat proper disk in the standard topological ball with its given end collar. Encode that standard ball, disk and finitely many pair charts as in [F7], apply the normal existence assertion of [F6] in $L[r]$, and export a compact tube with a wider domain and its actual boundary-collar certificates. Its zero-framing calculation and all subsequent Mayer–Vietoris and group pushout calculations are performed on the resulting actual objects in $V$. Thus no full-AC hypersurface supplier and no general homology-absoluteness assertion enters the no-choice Statement.

Write $P_0=P(U)$ and $R=\mathbb Z[1/|n|]$. First take the supplied smooth disk $D\subset B$. Apply the finite smooth disk-tube construction [F5] to this actual disk and its boundary collar. They give $N=D^2\times D^2$, product-shaped at its boundary. The framing at $P_0$ is zero. Indeed the small parallel disk is disjoint from $D$; boundary linking equals their intersection over $R$ in the $R$-homology ball. To check the latter identity here, two choices of bounding two-chain differ by a two-cycle, which bounds since $H_2(B;R)=0$; the chain intersection boundary formula makes their intersections with a proper relative cycle equal. Compare with the pushed-in boundary Seifert chain to get boundary linking. Thus the integral boundary linking is zero in $R$, hence zero in $\mathbb Z$. Put $Z=\overline{B\setminus N}$. Its boundary is the actual preferred-longitude filling $M(P_0)$. In the excisive collared decomposition $B=Z\cup N$, the overlap is $D^2\times S^1$. Mayer–Vietoris, with its connecting map represented by the meridian disk, gives $H_0(Z;R)=R$, $H_1(Z;R)=R[\mu_0]$ and $H_j(Z;R)=0$ for $j\ge2$. This uses only the stated $R$-homology of $B$. For a pseudo-slice disk the same construction applies smoothly with $R=\mathbb Z$. For a TOP disk this calculation is valid if its boundary-compatible zero-framed product normal neighborhood is actually supplied; this paragraph does not construct that neighborhood from local flatness.

Use the accepted actual standard infection cobordism [[lem-standard-infection-cobordisms-have-boundary-generated-second-homology]] for $P_0\cup\eta$ and $K$, with $\operatorname{lk}(P_0,\eta)=n$, and call it $E$. Its construction glues the two surgery products along the axis tube and companion filling solid torus, exchanging $\lambda_\eta=\mu_K$ and $\mu_\eta=\lambda_K$. Its third boundary is exactly $M(P(K))$, with its zero slope and oriented exterior marking, as proved in that supplier's2.1. Glue $Z$ to the $M(P_0)$ end, with the reversed boundary orientation needed to form the oriented cobordism $V$. Product collars make $V$ smooth for smooth input and TOP for supplied TOP tube input. The two remaining ends are $M(K)$ and $M(P(K))$. In $H_1(E;R)$ the incoming meridians and outgoing meridian have coordinates $(1,n,1)$, respectively for $P_0,K,P(K)$. In $H_2(E;R)=R^2$ the incoming classes are the coordinate basis and the outgoing class is $(1,n)$. These are the actual inclusion maps of the accepted supplier, not inferred solely from abstract ranks.

Here is the full gluing homology calculation. The common surgery $M(P_0)$ has $H_j=R$ in degrees0,1,2,3 and zero otherwise. The product-union spine defining $E$ has the Mayer–Vietoris sequence for the common solid torus; it gives $H_3(E;R)=R^2$ with the two incoming oriented fundamental classes as basis, $H_4(E;R)=0$, and no homology above4. This is the same finite sequence as the accepted supplier's3.1, now in degree3: the solid torus has no degree2 or3 homology. In the sequence for $V=E\cup_{M(P_0)}Z$, the degree3 map sends $1$ to the first basis vector of $R^2$; the degree2 map sends $1$ to the first basis vector of $R^2$; the degree1 map is the diagonal inclusion $R\to R\oplus R$ with unit coordinates, since $\mu_0$ generates both groups. All three are injective and the degree0 difference map is injective. Exactness in every degree therefore gives $H_j(V;R)=R$ for $j=0,1,2,3$ and zero otherwise. The $M(K)$ inclusion is an isomorphism in degree3 by the second fundamental-class coordinate, degree2 by the second basis coordinate, and degree1 by multiplication by $n$, a unit in $R$. For the outgoing end, degree2 is multiplication by $n$ because $(1,n)$ becomes $n$ in the quotient by the first basis vector; degree1 is the unit1. In degree3 the oriented boundary of a relative fundamental chain of $E$ is the sum of its incoming components minus the outgoing component. Consequently its outgoing degree3 class is the sum of the incoming classes; after gluing $Z$, it becomes the second generator. Degree0 is an isomorphism for both connected ends. Thus BOTH boundary inclusions are homology isomorphisms in every degree. The exact marked degree1 relation is $[\mu_K]=n[\mu_{P(K)}]$, with the signs determined by the supplied peripheral orientations. It is equality up to the unit $n$, not literal equality for general $n$. This is the precise meaning of the cited CFHH 'rel meridians' convention.

Suppose now that the supplied disk lies in a simply connected ball (standard TOP or pseudo-smooth) and that $P$ is strong winding $\pm1$. Van Kampen for $B=Z\cup N$ identifies $\pi_1B$ with $\pi_1Z/\langle\!\langle\mu_0\rangle\!\rangle$, so $\mu_0$ normally generates $\pi_1Z$. Strong winding says that $\eta$ normally generates the closure knot-complement group; its image therefore normally contains $\mu_0$ in $\pi_1Z$, since the knot exterior maps into $Z$. Hence $\eta$ normally generates $\pi_1Z$ too. The actual product-union construction of $E$ and van Kampen give $$\pi_1V=(\pi_1Z*\pi_1M(K))/\langle\!\langle\eta\mu_K^{-1}\rangle\!\rangle.$$ No injectivity of the gluing maps is assumed. Killing $\mu_K$ kills $\pi_1M(K)$ and then $\eta$, hence $\pi_1Z$; so $\mu_K$ normally generates $\pi_1V$. Killing $\mu_0$ instead kills $\pi_1Z$, hence $\eta=\mu_K$ and the other factor, so $\mu_0$ normally generates as well. The same $\mu_0$ is the outgoing satellite meridian in the actual infection boundary. Thus the image of either boundary group normally generates $\pi_1V$. The integer homology calculation is step3.1 with $n=\pm1$. The smooth pseudo-slice branch and the conditional supplied-neighborhood TOP branch follow with their actual categories; no smooth identification of a homotopy ball is used.

The smooth localized and pseudo-slice calculations in steps1.1–4.1 are unchanged, including both boundary homology maps and the signed relation $[\mu_K]=n[\mu_{P(K)}]$. For the arbitrary locally flat disk in the standard topological ball, [F6] now supplies the actual zero-framed product neighborhood that those same steps require. Their collar gluing, ordinary-coefficient Mayer–Vietoris sequences and van Kampen pushouts apply to this TOP neighborhood, so they prove the stated integral homology and normal-generation conclusions there too. No identification of a smooth homotopy ball with the standard smooth ball is used. All original category and closure hypotheses are retained.

Assume full AC, matching the chosen finite twisted-chain and maximal-abelian-cover conventions. Let K be a smooth oriented knot, M(K) its preferred-longitude zero-framed surgery, W a compact connected oriented smooth 4-manifold with boundary M(K), and π=π₁(W). Put π^(0)=π and π^(j+1)=[π^(j),π^(j)]. A right Zπ-chain complex with coefficients in a left Z[π/π^(j)]-module is formed by tensoring over Zπ with that module.

For n≥0, W is an integral n-solution for K when H₁(M(K);Z)→H₁(W;Z) is an isomorphism, H₂(W;Z) is free of rank 2r for some finite r, and there are classes x₁,…,x_r,y₁,…,y_r in H₂(W;Z[π/π^(n)]) whose equivariant intersection pairings satisfy λ_n(x_i,x_j)=0 and λ_n(x_i,y_j)=δ_ij. It is an integral (n+1/2)-solution when, in addition, each x_i is the image of a class x̃_i in H₂(W;Z[π/π^(n+1)]) and λ_{n+1}(x̃_i,x̃_j)=0 for all i,j. Here λ_j is the equivariant intersection pairing induced by the orientation of W.

For a commutative ring R with 1≠0, a group G belongs to Strebel's class D(R) if every homomorphism between projective RG-modules is injective whenever its tensor with the trivial G-module R is injective. In this page R is Q or F_p for a prime p. For a countable discrete group G, its group von Neumann algebra N G is the weak-operator closure of CG in the left regular representation on ℓ²(G), with trace τ_G(T)=⟨Tδ_e,δ_e⟩. The von Neumann dimension of a finitely generated projective N G-module represented by a projection E is τ_G(E); for an arbitrary module it is the supremum of the dimensions of its finitely generated projective submodules.

For a compact oriented 4-manifold W with boundary, sign(W) is the inertia difference of the symmetric intersection form on H₂(W;R) modulo its radical (the subspace pairing to zero with every class), equivalently on the image of H₂(W;R)→H₂(W,∂W;R). Given a closed oriented 3-manifold M, a homomorphism φ:π₁(M)→G, a compact oriented 4-manifold W with ∂W=M, and an extension ψ:π₁(W)→G of φ, the L²-signature sign_G^(2)(W,ψ) is the von Neumann signature of the nonsingular part of the N G-coefficient intersection form. When such a W and extension exist, the signature defect is sign_G^(2)(W,ψ)−sign(W). It is called the rho invariant of (M,φ) only after its independence of the bounding data is established by a separate bordism argument.

Assume AC. Let $G$ be a discrete group, let $A=\mathcal N G\subseteq\mathcal B(\ell^2(G))$ have its canonical faithful normal trace $\tau$, and give matrices the unnormalized trace $\tau_r((a_{ij}))=\sum_{i=1}^r\tau(a_{ii})$. For a projection $p\in M_r(A)$ put $\dim_A(pA^r)=\tau_r(p)$; for any right $A$-module take the supremum of dimensions of its finitely generated projective submodules. These dimensions are independent of the projective representation. If $L\subseteq pA^r$ is any submodule and $q$ is the projection onto its Hilbert closure in $p\ell^2(G)^r$, then $q\in M_r(A)$, $q\le p$, and
$$\dim_A L=\tau_r(q),\qquad \dim_A(pA^r/L)=\tau_r(p)-\tau_r(q).$$
In particular a Hilbert-dense submodule has dimension-zero quotient. Modules of dimension zero are closed under submodules, quotients, extensions and filtered colimits. For any matrix $B\in M_{r,s}(A)$, its kernel and Hilbert-closed image are projection modules, its algebraic image is isomorphic to its support projection module, and
$$\tau_s(P_{\ker B})+\tau_r(P_{\overline{\operatorname{im}B}})=s.$$

Work under the standing AC convention for finite von Neumann modules. Let $G$ be a countable discrete amenable group, so that for every finite $S\subseteq G$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a nonempty finite $F\subseteq G$ with $|SF\setminus F|<\varepsilon|F|$. Let $B\in M_{m,n}(\mathbb CG)$ act by left convolution on $\ell^2(G)^n$. The Hilbert closure of $\ker(B:(\mathbb CG)^n\to(\mathbb CG)^m)$ is the full Hilbert kernel of $B$. More precisely, if the finite coefficient support of $B$, together with the identity, is contained in $S$, and $K_F$ is the space of vectors in that kernel supported in $F$, then, writing $d=\tau_n(P_{\ker B})$ and $r=\tau_m(P_{\overline{\operatorname{im}B}})=n-d$,
$$n|F|-r|SF|\le\dim_{\mathbb C}K_F\le d|F|.$$
The closure of the right $\mathcal N G$-span of the algebraic kernel is therefore the full Hilbert kernel, and the quotient of the algebraic $\mathcal N G$-kernel by that span has dimension zero.

Let $A$ be a unital ring and $M$ a right $A$-module. Then the functor
$T_M=M\otimes_A-:A\text{-}\mathbf{Mod}\to\mathbf{Ab}$ is additive, preserves
cokernels (so it is right exact: every exact sequence
$X\xrightarrow fY\xrightarrow gZ\to0$ of left $A$-modules induces an exact
sequence $M\otimes_AX\xrightarrow{1\otimes f}M\otimes_AY\xrightarrow{1\otimes g}M\otimes_AZ\to0$),
and preserves arbitrary direct sums: the natural map
$\bigoplus_{i\in I}(M\otimes_AX_i)\to M\otimes_A(\bigoplus_{i\in I}X_i)$
induced by the coordinate inclusions is an isomorphism, including $I=\varnothing$.
If $M$ is a $(B,A)$-bimodule then $T_M$ takes values in left $B$-modules and all
the displayed maps are $B$-linear. No commutativity of $A$ or $B$ is assumed and
no choice is used.

For a right $R$-module $N$ with a specified projective resolution
$Q_\bullet\twoheadrightarrow N$ and a left $R$-module $M$, define the
right-resolution construction
$$\operatorname{Tor}^{R,Q}_n(N,M):=H_n(Q_\bullet\otimes_RM).$$
The datum $Q$ remains in the notation until the balance and change-of-resolution
results prove that it may be suppressed.

For every left $R$-module $M$, repeatedly taking the canonical free cover of the current kernel yields a functorial exact augmented complex of free modules $$\cdots\to F_2\to F_1\to F_0\to M\to0.$$ This construction is available in ZF because it uses only underlying sets and canonical free-module maps. Under the previously recorded choice boundary for free modules, the same complex is a projective resolution.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice.

Any two projective resolutions of the same object are homotopy equivalent over that object.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: First let $K\subseteq R^n$ be generated by finitely many columns, and let $B:R^s\to R^n$ be the corresponding matrix map onto $K$. Right exactness of tensor products identifies $K\otimes_R A$ with $A^s/\operatorname{im}((\ker_R B)\otimes_R A)$. The kernel of its natural map to $A^n$ is therefore $\ker_A B/\operatorname{im}((\ker_R B)\otimes_R A)$. This quotient has dimension zero by [F3]. The tensor-product identifications follow directly from the presentation $\ker_R B\to R^s\to K\to0$: relations among the chosen generators are exactly the elements of $\ker_R B$.

For an arbitrary submodule $K\subseteq R^n$, take its directed union of finitely generated submodules $K_j$. A tensor is a finite sum, so every element of $K\otimes_R A$ comes from some $K_j\otimes_R A$. If its image in $A^n$ is zero, its representative already lies in the kernel of the natural map $K_j\otimes_R A\to A^n$. Thus the kernel for $K$ is the directed union of images of the zero-dimensional kernels from step 1.1; it has dimension zero by [F2]. This also proves the assertion if relations identify different representatives, since images are quotients of those kernels.

Let $F=\bigoplus_{i\in I}R$ be any free module and $K\subseteq F$. Every finite tensor in $K\otimes_R A$ involves finitely many vectors of $K$, each of finite coordinate support in $F$. Their supports lie in one finite free summand $R^n\subseteq F$. A kernel element is therefore the image of a kernel for a submodule of that finite free summand, handled by step 2.1. Taking the directed union over those submodules and finite supports, and applying [F2], proves that $\ker(K\otimes_R A\to F\otimes_R A)$ has dimension zero for every free $F$.

Choose a free presentation $0\to K\to F\to M\to0$. In the resolution-dependent definition of Tor, first use a free resolution beginning with this presentation. For any other chosen projective resolution, [F5] gives chain maps inverse up to chain homotopy; this use of projective-resolution comparison relies on [A1]. Additive tensoring preserves the homotopy equation $f-g=dh+hd$, since tensoring respects sums and composition. Thus the tensor complexes are homotopy equivalent and their homology modules are isomorphic; the calculation below therefore applies to every retained resolution datum. A free resolution beginning with this presentation computes $\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,A)$ as $\ker(K\otimes_R A\to F\otimes_R A)$: resolving $K$ and splicing onto $F\to M$ gives this equality by right exactness at the last differential. Thus step 3.1 proves the assertion for degree one. For $q>1$, successively apply the same construction to the kernels in a free resolution of $M$; the positive-degree homology after splicing shifts by one, giving $\operatorname{Tor}_q^R(M,A)\cong\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(K_{q-1},A)$ for the appropriate syzygy $K_{q-1}$. The degree-one argument applies to every such module, so every asserted higher Tor group has dimension zero. No claim that these algebraic quotient modules are zero is used or obtained.

Assume AC. For every closed oriented smooth four-manifold $Z$ and every based homomorphism $\theta:\pi_1Z\to G$ to an arbitrary discrete group,
$$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(Z,\theta)=\operatorname{sign}(Z).$$
Let $M$ be a closed oriented smooth three-manifold and $\phi:\pi_1M\to G$ any homomorphism. There exist an injective homomorphism $j:G\hookrightarrow\Gamma$ and a compact oriented smooth four-manifold $W$ with $\partial W=M$ and a homomorphism $\pi_1W\to\Gamma$ restricting to $j\phi$. For any such data put
$$\rho_{\mathrm{sm}}(M,\phi)=\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_\Gamma(W)-\operatorname{sign}(W).$$
This number is independent of the smooth bound, its extending map and the injective target enlargement. The same value is obtained from $r$ copies of $M$ bounding a smooth $W$ by dividing its defect by $r>0$. Embedding the target group preserves the number. There is a finite constant $C_M$, depending only on the given smooth manifold $M$, such that
$$|\rho_{\mathrm{sm}}(M,\phi)|\le C_M$$
for all $G$ and $\phi$, including nononto homomorphisms and uncountable targets. For a disconnected compact $M$, use its finitely many components and the sum of these values, equivalently the free-product convention for its based fundamental groups. This is a signature-defect invariant among smooth bounds. No comparison with a nonsmooth TOP bound or an analytic eta definition is asserted.

Assume full AC. Let M be a closed oriented 3-manifold, Γ a discrete group, and φ:π₁(M)→Γ. If (W₀,ψ₀) and (W₁,ψ₁) are compact oriented 4-manifolds with boundary M over which φ extends, then sign_Γ^(2)(W₀,ψ₀)−sign(W₀)=sign_Γ^(2)(W₁,ψ₁)−sign(W₁). Hence the signature defect depends only on (M,φ).

derivations.claim: For smooth $M$, choose the one $W_M$ and degree-two presentation in [F2] before choosing a target or representation. For each $\phi:\pi_1M\to\Gamma$, functoriality of the acyclic envelope extends the representation over this same bound after the injective enlargement $\Gamma\hookrightarrow A(\Gamma)$. The actual coefficient chain-homotopy identities extend under the resulting ring homomorphism, so they still model its singular complex; no flatness of that homomorphism is needed. The extended degree-two term is the range of the same size-$N$ idempotent, of von Neumann dimension at most $N$. Its reduced homology and the positive and negative spectral subspaces have dimension at most $N$, hence $|\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_{A(\Gamma)}W_M|\le N$. Ordinary augmentation gives $|\operatorname{sign}W_M|\le N$ too. Independence in [F2] therefore yields $|\rho_{\mathrm{sm}}(M,\phi)|\le2N$, uniformly over every target cardinality and every homomorphism, including nononto maps. For finitely many components sum these constants; the empty manifold has constant zero.

For the literal TOP reading choose one compatible smooth structure on $M$ by [F3], once before choosing $\Gamma$ or $\phi$. Step1.1 supplies its finite constant $2N$. Any rho defined by a collared TOP bound agrees with the smooth bounding-defect value by [F3] and the bordism-independence lemma; thus the same constant bounds it. Finitely many connected components use the sum of their constants. This proves the full stated signature-defect convention with an explicitly external TOP comparison. It does not claim a new analytic eta-to-defect theorem for an unrelated definition of rho.

derivations.claim: First replace the term above degree $n$ by a finite free module if necessary. The image of $d_{n+1}$ after tensoring with $R$ is the kernel of $d_n$ over $R$, a finite-dimensional space. Choose finitely many tensors in $C_{n+1}\otimes R$ whose boundaries span it, and expand each tensor as a finite sum $c\otimes r$. The finitely many resulting elements $c\in C_{n+1}$ define a finite free module $P_{n+1}$ with a map to $C_{n+1}$; compose this map with $d_{n+1}$. Keep $P_i=C_i$ for $l\le i\le n$ and set all other terms to zero. Since $d_nd_{n+1}=0$, this defines a bounded finite-free complex $P_*$ whose $R$-homology vanishes through degree $n$. Below $n$ its $A$-homology is the original one, and in degree $n$ its $A$-homology surjects onto the original one, since it has the same cycles and possibly fewer boundaries. It suffices by [F3] to prove the result for $P_*$.

Over the field $R$, split the exact complex through degree $n$: choose vector-space complements of the kernels in each of its finitely many finite-dimensional terms, and invert each boundary map onto its image on the chosen complement. This gives maps $s_i:P_i\otimes R\to P_{i+1}\otimes R$, $l\le i\le n$, with $ds+sd=I$ through degree $n$. For $R=\mathbb F_p$, lift the finitely many matrix entries to integers and then to constant coefficients in $\mathbb Z\Gamma$, obtaining maps $D_i$. For $R=\mathbb Q$, choose a single positive integer $a$ clearing the denominators of all these finitely many matrices, and lift $a s_i$ instead; in the finite-field case put $a=1$. Set $D_i=0$ outside the indicated range. Then $f=dD+Dd$ is a chain map over $\mathbb Z\Gamma$, chain homotopic to zero, and its augmented matrix in degree $i\le n$ is $aI$, which is injective over $R$.

Apply [F1] to $f_i\otimes_{\mathbb Z}R$ on the free $R\Gamma$-module $P_i\otimes_{\mathbb Z}R$; its augmentation is injective by step 2.1, so this map is injective. Hence $f_i$ is injective over $\mathbb Z\Gamma$. For $R=\mathbb Q$ this follows by viewing a nonzero integral vector as a nonzero rational vector. For $R=\mathbb F_p$, an integral kernel vector has finitely many coefficients; divide them all by the largest common power of $p$. Torsion-freeness of the integral target preserves the kernel equation, and the resulting nonzero vector modulo $p$ contradicts injectivity. Passing to $\mathbb C\Gamma$ preserves this injection: any finite complex relation can be decomposed using a basis of the finite-dimensional rational span of its coefficients into rational relations, each of which clears denominators to an integral one.

Resolve the cokernel of the injective square matrix $f_i$ over $\mathbb C\Gamma$. The degree-one Tor group is the kernel of $f_i:A^{r_i}\to A^{r_i}$ after tensoring, where $r_i$ is the rank of $P_i$; this is the same free-presentation computation used to prove [F2]. Consequently [F2] makes that kernel dimension zero. Its projection has trace zero and is therefore zero by faithfulness in [F3]. Thus $f_i$ is injective on the Hilbert completion. Let $Z_i$ be the Hilbert kernel of $d_i$. The chain identity makes $f_i$ preserve $Z_i$. Its restriction to $Z_i$ has zero kernel, and polar decomposition in [F3] makes its Hilbert-closed image have the same trace dimension as $Z_i$; since that image lies in $Z_i$, faithfulness makes it dense in $Z_i$.

The algebraic $A$-cycle module is the projection module $P_{Z_i}A^{r_i}$ and is Hilbert-dense in $Z_i$ by [F3]. Let V=S¹×D² be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core, meridional disk and product longitude. A pattern is a smooth oriented knot P in the interior of V. Its winding number w(P) is its algebraic intersection with an oriented meridional disk, equivalently the coefficient of the core in [P]∈H₁(V;Z). For a smooth oriented knot K in S³, let e_K:V→S³ be a zero-framed tubular embedding carrying the core to K and carrying the meridian and product longitude to the positive meridian and preferred longitude of K. The satellite knot P(K) is e_K(P).

When concordance preservation has been established, the formula [K]↦[P(K)] defines a set map on each of C_sm, C_top, C_ex and C^{1/n}. The solid-torus meridian is strong winding number ±1 for P if, after V is embedded as the standard unknotted solid torus and P(U) denotes the resulting closure, that meridian normally generates π₁(S³\P(U)). Normal generation means that the smallest normal subgroup containing the element is the whole group. Strong winding number ±1 is a separate condition from ordinary winding number ±1. No additivity or homomorphism property is part of this definition.

Let P be an oriented pattern of winding n≠0 and K an oriented knot. If P(U) bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold B whose oriented boundary is identified with the standard oriented S³ and H_i(B;R_n)≅H_i(B⁴;R_n) for every i, then for every K the zero surgeries M(P(K)) and M(K) are smoothly R_n-homology cobordant. For the positive meridians determined by the supplied orientations, their images in the cobordism satisfy [mu_K]=n[mu_{P(K)}]; in particular they differ by a unit of R_n. This is a winding-unit meridian comparison, not a claim of literal equality for arbitrary winding. If P has strong winding number ±1 and P(U) is pseudo-slice (respectively locally flat topologically slice), then M(P(K)) and M(K) are smoothly (respectively topologically) homology cobordant through a 4-manifold whose fundamental group is normally generated by the image of the fundamental group of either boundary component. The category and closure hypotheses are separate and cannot be inferred from winding alone.

Let knots be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented S³ and let I=[0,1]. Let C_sm be their smooth concordance classes, where equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in S³×I. Let C_top be their locally flat topological concordance classes in that product. Let C_ex be their exotic-smooth concordance classes: equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W together with an orientation-preserving homeomorphism of pairs (W,∂W)≅(S³×I,S³×{0,1}) matching the endpoint knots. The annulus is oriented so that its boundary is −K₀ at the lower end and K₁ at the upper end, and it has product collars at both ends agreeing with the ambient boundary collars. For a nonzero integer n set R_n=Z[1/|n|]. Let C^{1/n} be the classes under equivalence witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W with boundary the two standard endpoint 3-spheres such that each boundary inclusion induces an isomorphism H_i(S³;R_n)→H_i(W;R_n) for every i. The annulus is oriented so that its boundary is −K₀ at the lower end and K₁ at the upper end, with product collars at both ends agreeing with the ambient boundary collars. A knot is pseudo-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold homeomorphic to B⁴, with its oriented boundary identified with the standard oriented S³. A knot is Z[1/|n|]-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold B with its oriented boundary identified with the standard oriented S³ and with H_i(B;R_n)≅H_i(B⁴;R_n) for every i; such a B is an R_n-homology 4-ball. These are sets of equivalence classes; this definition alone asserts no group structure.

Assume AC_ω. Under connected sum, each of C_sm, C_top, C_ex and C^{1/n} is an abelian group. The identity is the class of the unknot, and the inverse of [K] is the class of the reverse mirror of K. Each category retains the ambient and coefficient conditions in its definition.

Let B be a smooth 4-ball embedded in the standard smooth 4-sphere S⁴. The closure of S⁴\B is diffeomorphic to the standard 4-ball. This is the special smooth Schoenflies complement assertion used after a capped contractible 4-manifold has been identified with standard S⁴; it does not assert the smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture.

Let P be a pattern and let K be a knot. Choose a transverse meridional disk for P and a short product slab about it. Form a pattern P_K by replacing all strands of P across that slab by parallel untwisted copies of a long-knot representative of K, with the individual strand orientations inherited from P; this is simultaneous companion insertion, rather than tying K into just one arc. For every knot J, the satellite P(K#J) is isotopic as an oriented knot to P_K(J). The pattern P_K has the same winding number as P.

Let P⊂S¹×D² be a smooth oriented pattern. If oriented knots K₀ and K₁ are concordant in one of the four categories C_sm, C_top, C_ex or C^{1/n}, then P(K₀) and P(K₁) are concordant in the same category. Thus P induces a well-defined set map on each of these concordance sets.

Let A be a proper annulus in a compact oriented 4-manifold W, with boundary knots K₀ and K₁ in the two boundary 3-spheres. Assume A has an oriented normal disk neighborhood A×D² whose endpoint framings are the preferred zero-linking longitudes. Let R be Z or R_n=Z[1/|n|], and assume each end S³→W is an R-homology isomorphism. Removing A×D² and attaching D²×S¹×I along the annular side, with ∂D² matched to the annulus longitude and the core matched to the normal meridian, produces a cobordism V from M(K₀) to M(K₁). The statement predicts that the boundary inclusions M(K_i)→V are R-homology isomorphisms. If W is simply connected, it also predicts that π₁(V) is normally generated by either endpoint knot-group image.

Let P be a pattern of strong winding number ±1. For every oriented knot K, regard P(K) as the pattern obtained by tying K into each strand of P in the companion solid torus. Then this new pattern P(K) also has strong winding number ±1. A pattern obtained from any strong-winding pattern by taking connected sum with a local knot also has strong winding number ±1.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, let $B^4=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\lVert x\rVert^2\le1\}$ with boundary $S^3$. The oriented connected sum $K\#K^\dagger$ bounds a smooth properly embedded disk $D\subset B^4$ for which the squared radial function $\rho(x)=\lVert x\rVert^2$ restricts to a Morse function on the interior of $D$ with all critical points of index $0$ or $1$.

derivations.claim: Apply [F13] to the finite compact input for the branch at hand. For TOP the ambient product or ball is already standard; for the exotic branch its actual marked product/ball homeomorphism is given and is encoded in both directions. Use two coding passes. First encode only this finite compact geometry by a real $r_0$. In $L[r_0]$, before imposing any localized homology or strong-winding condition, use the ordinary finite smooth Morse construction to obtain finite handle/CW presentations of the supplied smooth ambient manifolds and finite presentations of the relevant knot exteriors, with their comparison maps, homotopies and peripheral markings. Export these purely geometric presentations and compact comparison certificates by [F13]. No choice-free generic-Morse theorem in $V$ is being assumed. Now work in $V$: its given localized homology hypothesis applies to these actual exported presentations. Over the PID $R_n$, the augmented finite free chain complex for an $R_n$-acyclic ball, or the mapping cone for either boundary inclusion, has a finite matrix contracting homotopy; finite row/column reduction supplies it. Likewise, the given strong-winding condition supplies, for each generator in the finite closure-knot presentation, an actual finite word expressing it as a product of conjugates of the designated axis meridian. There are only finitely many such generators and certificates, so choosing this list needs only finite choice. Enlarge $r_0$ to one real $r$ containing the presentations, their actual comparison certificates, these input group words and the finite contraction matrices. Their displayed equations $dh+hd=1$ and word identities are arithmetic, and establish the exact input homology and strong-winding hypotheses inside $L[r]$. No raw homology or fundamental-group absoluteness is asserted. In that model apply the unconditional CDR weak geometry, including [F11], [F12] and the finite connected-sum identities needed in [F4]. Export the resulting compact manifolds, disks, homeomorphisms and finite homology certificates using [F13]. Both stages carry finite normal-generation certificates: the input axis words just described accompany the final CDR call, and the output cobordisms are exported with explicit words expressing each generator in their finite presentations as a product of conjugates of the designated boundary generators. These are actual finite witnesses in $V$. The only ambient hypotheses in these applications are the actual coded ones, and no family of annuli or arbitrary points is selected. In the ordinary smooth branch export only the unconditionally constructed contractible smooth $B$ and its marked co-core; do not assume the ambient smooth Poincare hypothesis in $L[r]$. After decoding in $V$, cap the actual $B$ there, and only then use the supplied smooth Poincare hypothesis in step2.3.

Now suppose P(K)=P(J). By [F6], the connected-sum identity and the ribbon inverse give $P(J)=P_K(-K\#J)$ as concordance classes. Define R as the local connected sum of −P(K) with P_K. Then R(−K#J) is concordant to U because K#(−K#J) is concordant to J and satellites preserve concordance; moreover R(U)=−P(K)#P(K). By [F10], this closure is ribbon; [F6] gives w(R)=w(P).

Suppose P(K)=P(U), with the stated closure-slice hypothesis. By [F7] this equality is witnessed by a concordance annulus; the zero-surgery descent [F12], with the retained normal-GIVEN construction [F8], gives a meridian-preserving homology cobordism from M(P(K)) to M(P(U)). Applying [F2] to K and U gives cobordisms from M(P(K)) to M(K) and from M(P(U)) to M(U). On each pattern cobordism its marked first-homology relation is [mu_companion]=n[mu_satellite], where n is a unit in R_n; the concordance cobordism from [F8] identifies the two satellite meridian classes exactly. No equality of the pattern and companion preferred meridians is assumed.

Glue the cobordisms along the identified surgery manifolds. Mayer–Vietoris shows that the resulting boundary inclusions retain the required homology isomorphisms. In the exotic/topological branches, van Kampen shows the boundary normal-generation condition is preserved under this gluing. Hence M(K) and M(U) satisfy the corresponding surgery-cobordism relation. In the localized branch each endpoint meridian maps to a unit multiple of the same H_1 generator: compose the two winding-unit relations and the intervening exact concordance relation. In particular each endpoint meridian, including that of K, remains an R_n-module generator. In the strong-winding branches n=+1 or -1, so these multipliers are already integral units.

In the localized category, cap the M(U)=S¹×S² end with S¹×B³. Mayer–Vietoris gives an R_n-homology circle X with boundary M(K), and its meridian class is an R_n-module generator by step1.2. Attach a smooth 2-handle along that meridian with the surgery-dual zero framing. The relative pair (B,X) has only H_2(B,X;R_n)=R_n, generated by its core; its boundary map to H_1(X;R_n)=R_n is the meridian class, hence multiplication by a unit and an isomorphism. The pair sequence gives H_i(B;R_n)=0 for all i>0 and H_0(B;R_n)=R_n. The boundary handle description is the zero-surgery presentation for K together with its zero-framed meridian; this dual meridian surgery restores S³, and the 2-handle co-core has boundary K under that identification. Thus the resulting B is an R_n-homology ball containing the required smooth proper disk, proving K=U in C^{1/n}. Only a unit meridian multiplier was used, so the corrected [F2] supplies exactly the needed premise.

In the exotic and topological categories, the normal-generation condition makes the capped manifold after the meridian 2-handle contractible with boundary S³. The external input [F11] identifies this manifold with the boundary-marked topological $B^4$. Its co-core is smooth in the exotic branch and locally flat in the TOP branch, and its boundary is the original marked $K$. It therefore gives a pseudo-slice disk or a TOP slice disk respectively, proving $K=U$ in the required category.

In the ordinary smooth branch, work now in the ambient universe $V$: if P(U) is smoothly slice and P has strong winding ±1, the same cap and handle construction gives a contractible smooth 4-manifold B with boundary S³. Capping B with standard B⁴ gives a smooth homotopy S⁴; under the smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture and [F5], B is diffeomorphic to B⁴.

If P has strong winding ±1, [F9] implies R also has strong winding ±1. The closure R(U) supplies the localized slice, pseudo-slice, topological-slice, and standard smooth-slice hypotheses in their respective branches. Apply the applicable earlier weak-injectivity branch to R to obtain $-K\#J=U$ and hence $K=J$.
