Put π^(0)=π and π^(j+1)=[π^(j),π^(j)]. A right Zπ-chain complex with coefficients in a left Z[π/π^(j)]-module is formed by tensoring over Zπ with that module.

For n≥0, W is an integral n-solution for K when H₁(M(K);Z)→H₁(W;Z) is an isomorphism, H₂(W;Z) is free of rank 2r for some finite r, and there are classes x₁,…,x_r,y₁,…,y_r in H₂(W;Z[π/π^(n)]) whose equivariant intersection pairings satisfy λ_n(x_i,x_j)=0 and λ_n(x_i,y_j)=δ_ij. It is an integral (n+1/2)-solution when, in addition, each x_i is the image of a class x̃_i in H₂(W;Z[π/π^(n+1)]) and λ_{n+1}(x̃_i,x̃_j)=0 for all i,j. Here λ_j is the equivariant intersection pairing induced by the orientation of W.

For a commutative ring R with 1≠0, a group G belongs to Strebel's class D(R) if every homomorphism between projective RG-modules is injective whenever its tensor with the trivial G-module R is injective. In this page R is Q or F_p for a prime p. For a countable discrete group G, its group von Neumann algebra N G is the weak-operator closure of CG in the left regular representation on ℓ²(G), with trace τ_G(T)=⟨Tδ_e,δ_e⟩. The von Neumann dimension of a finitely generated projective N G-module represented by a projection E is τ_G(E); for an arbitrary module it is the supremum of the dimensions of its finitely generated projective submodules.

For a compact oriented 4-manifold W with boundary, sign(W) is the inertia difference of the symmetric intersection form on H₂(W;R) modulo its radical (the subspace pairing to zero with every class), equivalently on the image of H₂(W;R)→H₂(W,∂W;R). Given a closed oriented 3-manifold M, a homomorphism φ:π₁(M)→G, a compact oriented 4-manifold W with ∂W=M, and an extension ψ:π₁(W)→G of φ, the L²-signature sign_G^(2)(W,ψ) is the von Neumann signature of the nonsingular part of the N G-coefficient intersection form. When such a W and extension exist, the signature defect is sign_G^(2)(W,ψ)−sign(W). It is called the rho invariant of (M,φ) only after its independence of the bounding data is established by a separate bordism argument.

Supply a finite polygonal oriented disk-band Seifert-surface model and local ambient smooth roundings for a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, with compatible closed product tube, positive meridian $\mu$, preferred longitude $\lambda$, collars and peripheral paths. Put $X=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T=\partial X$, and let $M=X\cup_T V$ be its actual preferred zero-longitude surgery, oriented to extend $X$. Let $k=\mathbb Z$ or a commutative field, $R=k[t,t^{-1}]$, and let $F$ be its fraction field, so $F=\mathbb Q(t)$ when $k=\mathbb Z$. Use the associated based right coefficient systems sending $\mu$ to $t$ with transport by the inverse unit, and their standard parallel Hermitian form.

The actual maps induce isomorphisms
$$i_*:H_1(X;R)\cong H_1(M;R),\qquad j_*:H_1(X;R)\cong H_1(X,T;R).$$
The closed Bockstein–duality pairing $B_M$ is defined on the whole first homology and is nonsingular. On $X$ use the following explicit classical cocycle rule: take an integral $R^\vee$-valued two-cocycle $a$ whose cap class is $\overline{j_*x}$, take one whole $F^\vee$-valued one-cochain $b$ with $\partial^*b=a$, and set $B_X(x,y)=[b(y)]\in F/R$. Such primitives exist, this rule is independent of all representatives and choices, and
$$B_X(x,y)=B_M(i_*x,i_*y).$$
Thus it is the nonsingular exterior classical Blanchfield form with the same positive-meridian, positive-push and first-variable conjugate-linear conventions. Based axis classes in the exterior are carried to their actual surgery classes. The constructions commute with the rational and prime coefficient maps wherever the displayed forms are compared; no choice principle, arbitrary knot projection theorem or four-dimensional normal-neighborhood claim is assumed.

Assume AC. For an integer $h\ge0$ or a half-integer $h=n+1/2$, let $\mathcal F_h^{\mathrm{sm}}$ be the set of smooth concordance classes whose preferred-longitude zero surgery bounds an integral $h$-solution. Use the integral lifted-pair definition: $H_1$ is identified with the boundary meridian $\mathbb Z$, $H_2$ is free of rank $2r$, there are exactly $r$ zero/unit pairs over the indicated derived quotient, and at a half level the isotropic classes lift one further derived stage. Every smooth pattern preserves smooth knot concordance. Then $\mathcal F_h^{\mathrm{sm}}$ is a subgroup of smooth knot concordance, $\mathcal F_{h'}^{\mathrm{sm}}\subseteq\mathcal F_h^{\mathrm{sm}}$ for $h'\ge h$, and every smooth knot lies in $\mathcal F_0^{\mathrm{sm}}$.

More specifically, let $R$ be a smooth slice knot and let $\eta$ be a supplied unknotted infection axis in its exterior with $[\eta]\in\pi_1(S^3\setminus R)^{(k)}$, where $k\ge1$. For every smooth knot $J$, the infection $R(\eta,J)$ has an actual smooth integral $k$-solution. All constructions use finite smooth disk-band, peripheral product-tube, collar and path data; these data may be chosen under the stated AC.

Consequently, if $P$ is a winding-zero smooth pattern, then for every $k\ge1$ and every smooth knot $J$,
$$[P^k(J)]-[P^k(U)]\in\mathcal F_k^{\mathrm{sm}},\qquad \langle P^k(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{sm}})\rangle\subseteq\mathcal F_k^{\mathrm{sm}}+\langle[P^k(U)]\rangle.$$
No locally flat tubular neighborhood or TOP realization theorem is assumed or concluded.

Assume AC. Fix $n\ge1$ and a smooth winding-zero pattern $P$ whose axis has nonzero integral classical Blanchfield self-value, equivalently using the actual exterior-to-zero-surgery identification. Supply finite smooth disk-band models, peripheral product tubes, paths and compatible collars for the finitely many knots and infection pieces used below.

For every $m\ge1$ there are smooth knots $J_1,\ldots,J_m$ with explicit finite disk-band surfaces such that no nonzero signed connected sum
$$K=\mathop{\#}_{i=1}^m a_i P^n(J_i),\qquad (a_1,\ldots,a_m)\in\mathbb Z^m\setminus\{0\},$$
bounds a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold $V$ with collared boundary $M(K)$ and the following lifted half-pair data: boundary inclusion identifies $H_1(M(K);\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$ with $H_1(V;\mathbb Z)$, $H_2(V;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^{2r}$, there are exactly $r$ height-$n$ equivariant pairs $x_i,y_i$ with zero $x$-pairings and unit $x,y$-pairings, and the $x_i$ lift to height $n+1$ with zero pairings. Height $h$ means coefficients $\mathbb Z[\pi_1(V)/\pi_1(V)^{(h)}]$. Signed knots use the marked mirror-and-reverse inverse convention.

There is also one smooth knot $J$, with explicit finite disk-band surface, for which
$$P^n(J)\#P^n(J)\#\bigl(-P^n(J\#J)\bigr)$$
is not smoothly slice. More generally its zero surgery bounds no compact connected smooth integral homology-circle four-manifold with boundary-meridian $H_1$ isomorphism.

The coefficient maps and all signature sums used to obtain these obstructions are maps on the actual smooth bounding manifolds and infection pieces. No TOP-to-smooth rho comparison, choice-free analytic conclusion, integral-filtration subgroup construction, or quotient-rank conclusion is implicit in this supplied-data obstruction theorem.

Assume AC. Let $V$ be a compact connected oriented collared topological four-manifold with connected boundary $M$, with $H_1(M;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(V;\mathbb Z)$ the isomorphism $\mathbb Z[\mu]\to\mathbb Z[\mu]$ and $H_2(V;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^{2r}$. Supply $r$ ordinary zero/unit pairs $x_i,y_i$, and supply isotropic lifts of the $x_i$ to the abelian cover of $V$. Let $p$ be any prime, let $C_p$ be the cyclic group of order $p$, and let $\phi:\pi_1(V)\to\mathbb Z\to C_p$ send the meridian to its positive generator. Then
$$\operatorname{sign}_{C_p}^{(2)}(V,\phi)=\operatorname{sign}(V)=0.$$
The completed coefficient homology has $b_0^{(2)}(V)=b_1^{(2)}(V)=1/p$, $b_2^{(2)}(V)=2r$ and $b_3^{(2)}(V)=b_4^{(2)}(V)=0$, and the middle intersection form has zero radical. In particular, when $V$ is smooth, its boundary restriction has $\rho_{\mathrm{sm}}(M,\phi|_M)=0$. Every smooth integral $1$-solution satisfies the supplied pair hypotheses. No comparison between a nonsmooth TOP defect and a smooth bounding-defect invariant is asserted.

Assume AC. Let $P$ be a smooth winding-zero pattern whose axis has nonzero integral classical Blanchfield self-pairing in the Alexander module of $P(U)$. Let $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{sm}}$ denote smooth oriented knot concordance with its reverse-mirror inverse, and let $P^0$ be the identity. Then for every $n\ge0$ the abelian-group quotient
$$\langle P^n(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{sm}})\rangle/\langle P^{n+1}(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{sm}})\rangle$$
has infinite rational rank. For every $n\ge1$ the smooth satellite map $P^n$ is not a group homomorphism. The proof uses finite companion families depending on a prescribed rank bound; no infinite choice of an explicit independent sequence is required. No coprime Alexander-polynomial condition is imposed. This theorem retains full AC and makes no assertion identifying nonsmooth TOP defects with smooth bounding invariants.

Let $n\ge1$. Supply a compact connected oriented topological four-manifold $V$ with boundary a marked knot zero surgery, $H_1(V;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ and $H_2(V;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^{2r}$, and exactly $r$ integral pairs $x_i,y_i\in H_2(V;\mathbb Z[\pi/\pi^{(n)}])$, $\pi=\pi_1(V)$, satisfying $\lambda(x_i,x_j)=0$ and $\lambda(x_i,y_j)=\delta_{ij}$. Form $W$ by any finite sequence of the actual marked standard connected-sum and winding-zero infection cobordism adjunctions along outgoing knot-surgery components, including orientation reversals, using supplied smooth peripheral products and collars. Let $\phi:\pi_1(W)\to\Gamma$ have PTFA target and restrict on $V$ through $\pi/\pi^{(n)}$. Take $k=\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb F_p$ and put $A=k[\Gamma]$, with involutive Ore fraction division ring $K$ and the based standard parallel Hermitian structure.

The image pairs $\ell_i,d_i\in H_2(W;A)$ satisfy $\lambda(\ell_i,\ell_j)=0$ and $\lambda(\ell_i,d_j)=\lambda(d_j,\ell_i)=\delta_{ij}$. Their localized boundary-intersection cokernel has dimension at most $2r$. For each boundary component $M_0$ on which $\phi$ is nontrivial, $H_1(M_0;K)=0$, its coefficient Bockstein–duality linking form is defined, and its actual inclusion kernel is isotropic:
$$B_{M_0}(z,w)=0\quad\text{for all }z,w\in\ker\{H_1(M_0;A)\to H_1(W;A)\}.$$
Thus every boundary class with nonzero self-pairing survives in $H_1(W;A)$ and lies outside every isotropic submodule. If a component's coefficient image is cyclic, its form additionally has the nonsingularity furnished by the cyclic-image coefficient theorem; no unrestricted PTFA nonsingularity is asserted.

For a finite forest of iterated winding-zero infections with these initial data, suppose each top meridian generates $H_1(W_n;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ up to sign, and each pattern-axis integral classical self-pairing is nonzero. Use the actual intermediate $W_j$, rational mixed coefficients through index $n$, and one bottom field $\mathbb F_p$. For every odd prime outside the explicit finite exceptional set of the axis values, every branch meridian has a nonzero class in $P^{n-j}\pi_1(W_j)/P^{n-j+1}\pi_1(W_j)$, of infinite order when $j>0$ and order $p$ when $j=0$. All these conclusions hold for the supplied locally flat topological bordisms and smooth bordisms without a choice principle. Existence of the initial $V$ and its lifted pairs from a concordance relation is a separate hypothesis, as are analytic rho invariance and signature vanishing.

Assume full AC. Let $M$ be a compact oriented Hausdorff topological manifold with supplied boundary collar, and supply a based homomorphism on each component to a discrete group $G$, with compatible paths when maps or gluings are considered. Use $R=\mathbb CG$, with involution conjugating complex scalars and sending $g$ to $g^{-1}$, and its based right regular local system with standard parallel Hermitian form. Let $A=\mathcal NG$ have the canonical group trace. Then its singular coefficient complex has an actual bounded finite-projective $R$ chain-homotopy model. Absolute, relative and finite whole-component gluing diagrams admit such models and finite matrix comparison maps.

After extending these finite projective matrices to $\ell^2(G)$, write $\mathscr H_i(M)$ for completed reduced homology, with boundaries replaced by their Hilbert closures. If $p_Z,p_B$ are the cycle and boundary-closure projections in a finite ambient projection module, the corresponding algebraic reduced module is $P_i=(p_Z-p_B)A^r$, and
$$H_i(M;A)\twoheadrightarrow P_i\hookrightarrow\mathscr H_i(M)=(p_Z-p_B)\ell^2(G)^r.$$
The first map has dimension-zero kernel, and the second is injective with dense image and need not be onto. Pair and whole-component Mayer–Vietoris sequences are weakly exact on the completed modules. Oriented cap duality gives bounded mutually inverse maps on their completed reduced homology and cohomology, with the cap-boundary and restriction identities. These structures and the resulting spectral signature do not depend on the finite-projective model.

For a four-manifold the middle intersection form is the bounded Hermitian form defined by inverse relative cap duality, restriction and evaluation. Its Hilbert radical is the kernel of its self-adjoint operator. Its signature is the trace of the positive spectral projection minus the trace of the negative projection; no closed range or bounded inverse is required for a manifold with boundary. For a closed four-manifold its middle intersection operator is boundedly invertible.

Let $W_0,W_1$ be compact oriented topological four-manifolds, let $N$ be a union of entire closed boundary components, and glue the two marked copies of $N$ by an orientation-reversing identification and the supplied collars. Put $W=W_0\cup_N W_1$ and supply one compatible regular coefficient system on $W$. Other boundary components may remain. Then
$$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W)=\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W_0)+\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W_1),\qquad\operatorname{sign}(W)=\operatorname{sign}(W_0)+\operatorname{sign}(W_1).$$
Orientation reversal changes the corresponding sign. No finite CW type, triangulation, smoothing of a topological four-manifold, equality of ordinary and $L^2$ signatures on arbitrary closed manifolds, or analytic eta-to-defect comparison is asserted or assumed. For an arbitrary possibly uncountable $G$, the finite-matrix construction has the same dimensions and signatures as its countable coefficient image, so it agrees with the countable-group convention.

Assume full AC. Let $V$ be a compact connected oriented topological four-manifold with a supplied collar and connected boundary $M$, and choose a based loop $\mu\subset M$ such that
$$H_1(M;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu],\qquad H_1(M;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\cong}H_1(V;\mathbb Z),\qquad H_2(V;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^{2r}.$$
Put $\pi=\pi_1(V)$, take $n\ge0$, and supply classes $x_i,y_i\in H_2(V;\mathbb Z[\pi/\pi^{(n)}])$, $1\le i\le r$, satisfying $\lambda_n(x_i,x_j)=0$ and $\lambda_n(x_i,y_j)=\delta_{ij}$. Supply classes $\widetilde x_i\in H_2(V;\mathbb Z[\pi/\pi^{(n+1)}])$ mapping to $x_i$ with $\lambda_{n+1}(\widetilde x_i,\widetilde x_j)=0$. These are actual lifted half-pair data on the supplied manifold; existence of such a manifold or lifts is not asserted.

Let $k=\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb F_p$ for any prime $p$. Let $G$ be a discrete amenable group in $D(k)$ with $G^{(n+1)}=1$, and supply $\phi:\pi\to G$ such that $\phi(\mu)$ has infinite order. Use its based regular unitary local system and the finite-projective topological intersection convention. Then
$$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(V,\phi)=0=\operatorname{sign}(V),$$
so its actual bounding signature defect is zero. This applies to the full supplied locally flat topological category as well as smooth manifolds; no finite CW type, smoothing, closed-manifold ordinary-versus-$L^2$ index equality or rho bordism-independence theorem is assumed. If a separately applicable bordism-independence result identifies a rho invariant with this bounding defect, that invariant is consequently zero.

Assume full AC and a smooth winding-zero pattern $P$ whose axis has nonzero integral classical Blanchfield self-value. Use oriented zero surgery $M(K)$ and the first-positive-push Levine–Tristram signature function $\sigma_J$. Let $L>0$ exceed the uniform Cheeger–Gromov bound for every rho value of $M(P(U))$ under every group representation. For every $n,m\ge1$, there are distinct odd primes $p_1,\ldots,p_m$ outside the finite exceptional set for reduction of this self-value and finite disk-band companion knots $J_i$ such that, writing $\zeta_p=\exp(2\pi i/p)$,
$$D_i=\frac1{p_i}\sum_{r=0}^{p_i-1}\sigma_{J_i}(\zeta_{p_i}^{r})>mnL,$$
with $\sigma_{J_i}(1)=0$, $\sigma_{J_i}(\zeta_{p_i})=\sigma_{J_i}(\zeta_{p_i}^{-1})>p_i mnL/2$, all other nonidentity $p_i$-th-root signatures zero, and every $p_j$-th-root signature zero for $j\ne i$. Thus $D_i$ is the canonical $\mathbb Z/p_i$ cyclic defect of $M(J_i)$. In any candidate smooth bounding bordism for a nonzero integer vector $(a_i)$ used in the actual finite-prime infection obstruction assembly, choose $i_*$ with $|a_{i_*}|=\max_i|a_i|$. Its supplied quotient using $p_{i_*}$ gives signed bottom boundary contribution $a_{i_*}D_{i_*}$; the remaining $n\sum_i|a_i|$ pattern terms have total absolute value less than $nL\sum_i|a_i|\le nmL|a_{i_*}|<|a_{i_*}|D_{i_*}$. Thus the total signed boundary rho value has the sign of $a_{i_*}$ and is nonzero.

For every $n\ge1$, the three-branch obstruction assembly also admits a finite disk-band companion knot with a canonical cyclic defect $D>3nL$. For any supplied candidate smooth homology-circle bound in that assembly, its quotient kills the distinguished negative bottom branch and gives either $0$ or $D$ on each positive bottom branch, with at least one value $D$. Its $3n$ remaining pattern terms have total absolute value less than $3nL$, so the total boundary rho value is positive. For a locally flat TOP pair-family application, the initial bordism must supply the actual height-$n$ pairs and height-$(n+1)$ isotropic lifts; for a TOP three-branch application it must supply the actual homology-circle bound. In either case the finite-projective coefficient quotient must satisfy the stated survival and vanishing hypotheses, and the boundary rho values must agree with the smooth bounding defects by the closed TOP bordism equality. Pairwise relatively prime Alexander polynomials belong only to the separate Theorem C comparison of distinct patterns; they are not hypotheses of Theorems A or B.

Assume full AC. Let M be a closed oriented 3-manifold, Γ a discrete group, and φ:π₁(M)→Γ. If (W₀,ψ₀) and (W₁,ψ₁) are compact oriented 4-manifolds with boundary M over which φ extends, then sign_Γ^(2)(W₀,ψ₀)−sign(W₀)=sign_Γ^(2)(W₁,ψ₁)−sign(W₁). Hence the signature defect depends only on (M,φ).

Assume full AC. For every closed oriented 3-manifold M there exists a finite constant C_M such that for every discrete group Γ and every homomorphism φ:π₁(M)→Γ for which the rho invariant is defined, |ρ(M,φ)|≤C_M. The constant may depend on M but not on Γ or φ.

Assume AC. Let $V$ be a compact connected oriented collared topological four-manifold with connected boundary $M$, with $H_1(M;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(V;\mathbb Z)$ the isomorphism $\mathbb Z[\mu]\to\mathbb Z[\mu]$ and $H_2(V;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^{2r}$. Supply $r$ ordinary zero/unit pairs $x_i,y_i$, and supply isotropic lifts of the $x_i$ to the abelian cover of $V$. Let $p$ be any prime, let $C_p$ be the cyclic group of order $p$, and let $\phi:\pi_1(V)\to\mathbb Z\to C_p$ send the meridian to its positive generator. Then
$$\operatorname{sign}_{C_p}^{(2)}(V,\phi)=\operatorname{sign}(V)=0.$$
The completed coefficient homology has $b_0^{(2)}(V)=b_1^{(2)}(V)=1/p$, $b_2^{(2)}(V)=2r$ and $b_3^{(2)}(V)=b_4^{(2)}(V)=0$, and the middle intersection form has zero radical. In particular, when $V$ is smooth, its boundary restriction has $\rho_{\mathrm{sm}}(M,\phi|_M)=0$. Every smooth integral $1$-solution satisfies the supplied pair hypotheses. No comparison between a nonsmooth TOP defect and a smooth bounding-defect invariant is asserted.

Supply distinct odd primes $p_1,\ldots,p_m$ with $m\ge1$ and positive real numbers $C_1,\ldots,C_m$. Put $\omega_j=\exp(2\pi i/p_j)$. A finite construction gives smooth oriented knots $K_1,\ldots,K_m$, each with a supplied connected one-boundary oriented Seifert surface and ordered integral basis with exact positive-push matrix $V_i$. Define its chosen-surface signature function by
$$s_i(z)=\operatorname{sign}\bigl((1-z)V_i+(1-\bar z)V_i^T\bigr),\qquad z\in S^1.$$
There are positive integers $N_i$ such that
$$s_i(\omega_i)=s_i(\omega_i^{-1})=2N_i>C_i,$$
while $s_i(\omega_i^r)=0$ when $r\not\equiv\pm1\pmod{p_i}$, and $s_i(\omega_j^r)=0$ for all integers $r$ when $j\ne i$. Each $s_i$ is nonnegative on the entire unit circle. In particular,
$$\frac1{p_i}\sum_{r=0}^{p_i-1}s_i(\omega_i^r)=\frac{4N_i}{p_i}>\frac{2C_i}{p_i},\qquad \frac1{p_j}\sum_{r=0}^{p_j-1}s_i(\omega_j^r)=0\quad(j\ne i).$$
The surface for $K_i$ has genus $4N_i$. No choice principle, concordance classification, cabling formula, signature-to-rho formula or uniform analytic bound is assumed.

Assume AC. For every supplied finite smooth oriented disk-band Seifert surface $F$ with one-boundary knot $K$, ordered homology basis and first-variable positive-push matrix $V$, let $W_F$ and its meridional extension $\psi_d:\pi_1(W_F)\to\mathbb Z/d$ be the actual construction of the finite disk-band bounding-manifold construction. For every positive integer $d$, set $\zeta_d=\exp(2\pi i/d)$ and
$$D_d(F)=\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_{\mathbb Z/d}(W_F,\psi_d)-\operatorname{sign}(W_F).$$
Then
$$D_d(F)=\frac1d\sum_{r=0}^{d-1}\operatorname{sign}\bigl((1-\zeta_d^r)V+(1-\zeta_d^{-r})V^T\bigr).$$
The sign is exactly the positive $L^2$ signature minus ordinary signature convention. The formula allows singular character forms and all $d$, including $d=1$ and even $d$. The term $r=0$ is defined by the zero Hermitian matrix and contributes zero; its equality to the trivial-character signature follows from the ordinary metabolic calculation, not from specialization of a localized homology basis.

The boundary is the actual oriented zero surgery and its positive meridian map, not the knot exterior or a simply connected trace. The displayed formula proves this **canonical bounding defect**. Whenever a separately proved applicable bordism-independence assertion identifies the rho invariant with the defect of this bounding extension, it consequently gives the same value for that rho invariant. No such general independence assertion, global signature invariance, rho identification, uniform bound, infinite-cyclic formula or arbitrary-group index theorem is asserted here.

derivations.claim: In the smooth category [F1] identifies the stipulated nonzero classical axis self-value with exactly the integral surgery self-value used in [F4]. The winding and orientation conventions are the same, and AC verifies its actual geometric and analytic hypotheses. Apply [F4] to obtain infinite rational rank of $\langle P^n(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{sm}})\rangle/\langle P^{n+1}(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{sm}})\rangle$ for every $n\ge0$, including its separate finite-cyclic proof at $n=0$. Its finite families are chosen for each desired rank bound, so no assertion of a single explicit infinite independent sequence is needed. This establishes the entire smooth rank branch of the original Statement.

Work in the TOP group of [F8]. Fix $n\ge1$ and any desired finite rank $m$. Choose the finite family in [F6] for size $m+1$. If a nonzero signed sum of its $P^n$ iterates belonged to $\mathcal F_{n+1}^{\mathrm{top}}$, its defining TOP solution would have exactly the integral height-$n$ pairs and isotropic height-$(n+1)$ lifts needed by [F5]. The finite forest quotient maps in [F5] have amenable target in the specified $D(k)$ class, with top meridian of infinite order. The accepted TOP half-pair theorem gives zero defect of that actual solution; the smooth standard joining/infection pieces have zero defect as well. Whole-component additivity makes the actual boundary defect sum zero. But [F6] evaluates its bottom terms by canonical cyclic numbers and gives strict signed domination over all pattern terms. This is a contradiction. Thus these $m+1$ classes are rationally independent modulo $\mathcal F_{n+1}^{\mathrm{top}}$: a rational relation clears denominators to the excluded nonzero signed integer relation.

At $n=0$, take any finite family of the signature bumps in [F7], with distinct selected primes. For a nonzero signed sum choose an index with nonzero coefficient and evaluate the canonical cyclic defect at that prime. All cross-prime terms vanish, so the value is the selected nonzero integer coefficient times its positive normalized mean. It cannot vanish. A TOP integral1-solution would give an integral half-solution at height0 and force the same defect to vanish by [F7] and [F6]. These classes are therefore independent modulo $\mathcal F_1^{\mathrm{top}}$. Since $\langle P(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{top}})\rangle\subset\mathcal F_1^{\mathrm{top}}+\langle P(U)\rangle$, the same at-most-one rank loss proves infinite rank of $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{top}}/\langle P(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{top}})\rangle$.

For $n\ge1$, [F4] also gives a knot $J$ for which $P^n(J)\#P^n(J)\#(-P^n(J\#J))$ is not smoothly slice. A homomorphism on smooth concordance would make this class zero, contradicting the actual witness. Thus the entire smooth nonhomomorphism branch follows as well. Neither [F4]'s rank proof nor this witness uses a pairwise-coprime Alexander-polynomial condition, so the original A/B scope is retained.

By [F8], $\langle P^{n+1}(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{top}})\rangle$ lies in $\mathcal F_{n+1}^{\mathrm{top}}+\langle P^{n+1}(U)\rangle$. Quotienting a rational vector space by the span of one element loses at most one dimension. Step3.1 therefore gives rank at least $m$ for the image of $\langle P^n(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{top}})\rangle$ modulo that larger subgroup, hence also for its quotient by $\langle P^{n+1}(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{top}})\rangle$. Since $m$ was arbitrary, the rank is infinite. This uses finite families of each requested size, not an unproved explicit infinite sequence.

For $n\ge1$, choose the three-branch companion in [F6] with normalized positive cyclic defect exceeding $3nL$. If $P^n(J)\#P^n(J)\#(-P^n(J\#J))$ were TOP slice, [F8] would give an actual collared TOP homology-circle disk exterior. This is the zero-pair case of [F5], and its three-branch quotient kills the distinguished negative bottom restriction while at least one positive bottom restriction has the required cyclic order. The actual half-pair zero defect and piecewise gluing force total defect zero, while [F6] gives a strictly positive bottom sum exceeding all $3n$ pattern terms. This contradiction proves the TOP nonhomomorphism witness. Steps1.1–2.1 already supplied the smooth conclusions. No coprime Alexander hypothesis was used. The full original Statement follows, with precisely the TOP geometric foundations and closed TOP equality declared external.

Let V=S¹×D² be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core, meridional disk and product longitude. A pattern is a smooth oriented knot P in the interior of V. Its winding number w(P) is its algebraic intersection with an oriented meridional disk, equivalently the coefficient of the core in [P]∈H₁(V;Z). For a smooth oriented knot K in S³, let e_K:V→S³ be a zero-framed tubular embedding carrying the core to K and carrying the meridian and product longitude to the positive meridian and preferred longitude of K. The satellite knot P(K) is e_K(P).

When concordance preservation has been established, the formula [K]↦[P(K)] defines a set map on each of C_sm, C_top, C_ex and C^{1/n}. The solid-torus meridian is strong winding number ±1 for P if, after V is embedded as the standard unknotted solid torus and P(U) denotes the resulting closure, that meridian normally generates π₁(S³\P(U)). Normal generation means that the smallest normal subgroup containing the element is the whole group. Strong winding number ±1 is a separate condition from ordinary winding number ±1. No additivity or homomorphism property is part of this definition.

derivations.claim: A cochain $f:C_1\to N$ is a cocycle precisely when $f(B_1)=0$. Restricting to $Z_1$ therefore induces a map $H_1=Z_1/B_1\to N$. A coboundary $g d_1$ vanishes on $Z_1$, so this induces the stated well-defined map $\kappa$. It is onto if every map $Z_1\to N$ vanishing on $B_1$ extends to $C_1$. It is injective if every map $B_0\to N$ extends to $C_0$: indeed a cocycle restricting to zero on $Z_1$ factors uniquely through $d_1:C_1\to B_0$, and such an extension expresses it as a coboundary.

For the principal-right-ideal alternative, $N$ is right divisible: given $n=q+R\in N$ and $0\ne a\in R$, the element $q a^{-1}+R$ multiplied on the right by $a$ equals $n$. We prove by induction on $m$ that any right-linear map $f:S\to N$ from any right submodule $S\subseteq R^m$ extends to $R^m$. For $m=0$ this is immediate. Let the projection of $S$ to the last coordinate be the right ideal $J$. If $J=0$, apply induction on the first $m-1$ coordinates and give the last basis vector value zero. Otherwise write $J=aR$ with $a\ne0$ and take $z=(z',a)\in S$. Then $S=S'\oplus zR$, where $S'=S\cap(R^{m-1}\times0)$: subtract $zr$ from an element with last coordinate $ar$, and uniqueness follows from the absence of zero divisors.

If $H_0=0$, then $d_1:C_1\to C_0$ is onto. Lift the finitely many given basis vectors of $C_0$ and extend linearly to a section $s:C_0\to C_1$. This gives $C_1=Z_1\oplus s(C_0)$. Extend a map from $Z_1$ by zero on the second summand to prove surjectivity in step 1.1. Here $B_0=C_0$, so the extension required for injectivity is automatic. The section uses only finitely many selections.

Extend $f|_{S'}$ to $g:R^{m-1}\to N$ by induction. Right divisibility supplies $v\in N$ with $va=f(z)-g(z')$. Define the extension on $R^m$ by $(u,r)\mapsto g(u)+vr$. It agrees with $f$ on $S'$ and on $z$, hence on all of $S$. This completes the finite induction, using one ideal generator, one lift, and one division at each of finitely many stages. It does not use a maximal extension argument or an infinite family of choices.

Apply the extension result of step 2.2 first to $Z_1\subseteq C_1$ and then to $B_0\subseteq C_0$, using the supplied finite bases. These are exactly the surjectivity and injectivity requirements of step 1.1. The first alternative was established in step 2.1, so $\kappa$ is an isomorphism in either case. Restriction and passage to cycles commute with every compatible left coefficient action; thus the inverse, being unique, also respects that action.

derivations.claim: A degree-one cocycle is a map $f:C_1\to N$ vanishing on $B_1$, and a coboundary is a map of the form $g d_1$. Restriction of a cocycle to $Z_1$ descends to $Z_1/B_1=H_1$; coboundaries restrict to zero. Thus restriction defines the stated map. If $a=0$, then $Z_1=C_1$ and all coboundaries vanish, so the map is already an isomorphism.

Suppose $a\ne0$. Choose $z\in C_1$ with $d_1z=a$. Because $R$ has no zero divisors, $aR\to C_1$, $ar\mapsto zr$, is well-defined and a section of $d_1$. Hence $C_1=Z_1\oplus zR$. Any map $H_1\to N$ pulls back to a map on $Z_1$ vanishing on $B_1$ and extends by zero on $zR$ to a degree-one cocycle. This proves surjectivity.

If a degree-one cocycle restricts to zero on $Z_1$, it factors as $v d_1$ for a right-linear map $v:aR\to N$. Let $v(a)=q+R$ with $q\in K$ and put $u=q a^{-1}+R$. Then $ua=v(a)$ in $N$. The right-linear map $g:R\to N$, $g(r)=ur$, extends $v$, since $g(ar)=v(a)r=v(ar)$. The cocycle is consequently the coboundary $g d_1$. This proves injectivity and the result. Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair and $\mathcal L$ a left $R$-module local system on $X$. The cellular local chain complex computes singular local homology:
$$H_n\bigl(C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H_n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$
The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms. Intrinsically,
$$C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\cong H_n(X^n\cup A,X^{n-1}\cup A;\mathcal L).$$
If a basepoint and one oriented lift of each cell outside $A$ are supplied on every component, the $n$th group is the direct sum of the corresponding coefficient fibers, and its boundary is the signed $R[\pi]$ incidence matrix acting through monodromy.

derivations.claim: The group $\Gamma$ is torsion-free abelian, hence PTFA with its one-step series. The ring $\Lambda$ is a commutative domain: after multiplying nonzero Laurent polynomials by monomials, lexicographically leading nonzero terms of ordinary polynomials have nonzero product over $\mathbb Z$. Its fraction field is $K$. Give each circle its one-vertex, one-edge cell structure, use their eight product cells on $T^3$, and lift them to the oriented coordinate cells of $\mathbb R^3$. Opposite faces differ by $x,y,1$, respectively. Thus [F1] identifies the coefficient complex with the exterior algebra on $e_1,e_2,e_3$, with differential the graded derivation $d(e_1)=a$, $d(e_2)=b$, $d(e_3)=0$. In particular $d_1(u,v,w)=au+bv$ and $d_2(p,q,r)=(-bp,ap,aq+br)$ in the ordered bases $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(e_1\wedge e_2,e_1\wedge e_3,e_2\wedge e_3)$.

Evaluation at $x=1$ identifies $\Lambda/(a)$ with the domain $\mathbb Z[y^{\pm1}]$; its kernel is exactly $(a)$ by multiplying by a power of $x$ and applying the ordinary identity $x^j-1=(x-1)(1+\cdots+x^{j-1})$. If $au+bv=0$, reduction modulo $a$ gives $b\bar v=0$, whence $v=at$ and $u=-bt$. Therefore every degree-one cycle has a unique expression $(-bt,at,w)$. The image of $d_2$ consists precisely of those expressions with arbitrary $t=p$ and $w\in I$. Consequently $H_1(M;\Lambda)\cong\Lambda/I\cong\mathbb Z$, generated by the third circle. It is nonzero, and all of it is $\Lambda$-torsion because $a\ne0$ annihilates it.

Over $K$, multiplication by $a$ is invertible. The operator $h(\omega)=a^{-1}e_1\wedge\omega$ satisfies $dh+hd=1$ by the displayed graded-derivation differential. Hence the entire coefficient chain complex over $K$ is contractible and in particular $H_1(M;K)=0$. This verifies the vanishing assumption of the refuted statement without any finiteness or rank inference.

Any $\Lambda$-linear map $\Lambda/I\to K/\Lambda$ is determined by the image $q+\Lambda$ of $1+I$, where $aq,bq\in\Lambda$. Set $r=aq$ and $s=bq$. Then $br=as$. Reducing this identity modulo $a$ and using the domain $\Lambda/(a)$ from step 2.1 gives $r=at$ for some $t\in\Lambda$. Since $a\ne0$ in the field $K$, the identity $aq=at$ forces $q=t\in\Lambda$. Thus the image of $1+I$ is zero, and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Lambda}(\Lambda/I,K/\Lambda)=0$. The conjugate dual is also zero; the involution $x\mapsto x^{-1},y\mapsto y^{-1}$ preserves $I$ because $x^{-1}-1=-x^{-1}a$ and $y^{-1}-1=-y^{-1}b$.

By steps 2.1 and 3.1, the adjoint of any sesquilinear pairing on $TH_1(M;\Lambda)$ with target $K/\Lambda$ has nonzero source and zero target, and therefore is not an isomorphism. This includes the coefficient Bockstein–duality pairing whenever expressed in those conventions. Together with step 2.2 this refutes the asserted implication. Every object and calculation is explicit and finite; no choice assumption is needed.

Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff manifold, $o\in M$, and $R$ a unital ring. One can construct paths $\gamma_x$ from $o$ to every $x\in M$, with $\gamma_o$ constant, by fixed rules from one finite atlas and finitely many connecting paths. Let $\mathcal R$ be a right-$R$ local system with a supplied identification $\mathcal R_o=R$ and transport given by left multiplication by units, with monodromy image $H\le R^\times$. Its twisted singular complex has an explicit chain decomposition $C_*(M;\mathcal R)=C'_*\oplus Q_*$ after a change of free bases, where $C'_0=R$, $C'_* $ is free, and $Q_*$ is contractible with its only nonzero differential an identity from degree one to degree zero. Moreover
$$\operatorname{im}(d'_1)=\sum_{h\in H}(h-1)R.$$
The decomposition and its dual cochain homotopy equivalences require no choice principle. In particular this image is principal if $H$ is cyclic, if it equals $R$, or if every right ideal of $R$ is principal.

Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff topological manifold and $o\in M$. There is a finite based graph mapped continuously into $M$ such that its induced fundamental-group map is onto. Consequently $\pi_1(M,o)$ has a finite generating list, without a choice principle. No triangulation or smooth structure on $M$ is assumed.

Let $\mathcal L$ be a left $R$-module local system on $X$ and let $A\subseteq X$. Since the differentials square to zero by [[lem-twisted-boundaries-square-to-zero-and-are-independent-of-lift-bases]], define
$$H_n(X,A;\mathcal L)=H_n\bigl(C_*^{\mathrm{sing}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr),\qquad H^n(X,A;\mathcal L)=H^n\bigl(C^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr),$$
using the relative complexes of [[def-singular-and-cellular-chain-complexes-with-local-coefficients]]. Write $H_n(X;\mathcal L)$ and $H^n(X;\mathcal L)$ when $A=\varnothing$. Negative-degree groups are zero.

For a connected CW pair, the universal-cover tensor and equivariant-Hom models in the same definition compute these groups once their chain comparison is established below. The intrinsic definition itself applies to arbitrary spaces and never assumes that a universal cover exists. On a disconnected space, chains and homology split as direct sums over components, while cochains form the degreewise product complex described in the preceding definition. Its cohomology is, by definition, the quotient of the kernel by the image in that product complex. No identification with the product of the component cohomology groups is asserted in ZF: surjectivity of that comparison can require simultaneously choosing componentwise primitives.

If $\underline M$ is the constant system with fiber an $R$-module $M$, every transport in the intrinsic formulas is the identity. Sending $m\sigma$ to the ordinary coefficient chain and reading a cochain as an arbitrary simplex function gives literal chain and cochain isomorphisms
$$C_*(X,A;\underline M)\cong C_*(X,A;M),\qquad C^*(X,A;\underline M)\cong C^*(X,A;M).$$
Thus constant local coefficients recover ordinary singular homology and cohomology with coefficients in $M$, including empty spaces, zero coefficients, points, and relative pairs.

derivations.claim: Fix the paths from [F1]. For a degree-one cocycle $\alpha$ in a local system $\mathcal E$, the two-simplex identity of [F2] gives $\alpha(uv)=\alpha(u)+T_u^{-1}\alpha(v)$ for concatenated paths, with the second term transported to the initial fiber. A triangle realizing the concatenation proves this formula, and a triangulated homotopy square proves invariance for endpoint-fixed path homotopies; common internal edges cancel with their inverse transports. A constant two-simplex shows that a cocycle evaluates to zero on a constant path, and the concatenation formula then handles reversed paths. Define a zero-cochain $v_x=T_{\gamma_x}\alpha(\gamma_x)$ and $v_o=0$. The normalized cocycle $\alpha^0=\alpha-\delta v$ vanishes on every $\gamma_x$. If $g_\sigma=[\gamma_x\sigma\overline\gamma_y]$ for a path $\sigma:x\to y$, the concatenation formula consequently gives $\alpha^0(\sigma)=T_{\gamma_x}d(g_\sigma)$, where $d(g)=\alpha^0(g)$ on based loops. Here $d(gh)=d(g)+\rho(g)d(h)$ with $\rho(g)=T_g^{-1}$ in the cohomological convention. This is a crossed homomorphism; conversely that formula assigns a normalized cocycle to every such $d$, since the three edges of a singular two-simplex satisfy the same loop relation.

Apply step 1.1 to a $\mathcal C$-cocycle. Choose one lift $b_s\in\mathcal B_o$ of $d(s)$ for each of the finitely many generators $s$ of $\pi_1(M,o)$ from [F1]. For its inverse use $b_{s^{-1}}=-\rho(s^{-1})b_s$. Order the finite alphabet and use shortlex order on its finite words. Every group element $g$ has a least representing word $w(g)$; the identity has the empty word. On a word $t_1\cdots t_k$ form the finite sum $D(w)=\sum_j\rho(t_1\cdots t_{j-1})b_{t_j}$ in $\mathcal B_o$, and put $Q(g)=D(w(g))$. Its image in $\mathcal C_o$ is $d(g)$ by the crossed-homomorphism law. Thus $b(\sigma)=T_{\gamma_x}^{\mathcal B}Q(g_\sigma)$ gives an actual $\mathcal B$-valued one-cochain lifting $\alpha^0$ on every singular path, without selecting a fraction representative for each path. Its coboundary has zero $\mathcal C$-image, so unique inverse images under the injective fiber maps $i$ define a two-cochain $a$ in $\mathcal A$ with $i(a)=\delta b$. It is a cocycle since $i$ is injective and $\delta^2b=0$. Define $\beta[\alpha]=[a]$.

Any other lift of the same normalized one-cochain differs from $b$ by the image of a unique $\mathcal A$-valued one-cochain, so its coboundary gives the same class $[a]$. This includes changes in the finite generators, their lifts and the shortlex order. If $\alpha$ is changed by $\delta c$ for a $\mathcal C$ zero-cochain, its normalization changes by $\delta\widehat c$, where $\widehat c_x=T_{\gamma_x}c_o$: indeed the change in the normalizing zero-cochain is $c_x-T_{\gamma_x}c_o$. A single lift of $c_o$ in $\mathcal B_o$, transported along all $\gamma_x$, lifts $\widehat c$. Its coboundary adjusts $b$ without changing $\delta b$. Thus $\beta$ depends only on the cohomology class. Sums of lifts are lifts of sums, and their coboundaries add, proving additivity.

The map also does not depend on the finite-atlas path assignment. Compare a second family $\eta_x$ with $\gamma_x$, and first use the $\gamma$-normalized cocycle. Its evaluation on $\eta_x$ is $d(k_x)$, where $k_x=[\eta_x\overline\gamma_x]$. Thus its $\eta$-normalizing zero-cochain is $T_{\eta_x}^{\mathcal C}d(k_x)$. The explicit $\mathcal B$ zero-cochain $T_{\eta_x}^{\mathcal B}Q(k_x)$ lifts it, so subtracting its coboundary from $b$ produces a lift of the $\eta$ normalization with the same two-coboundary. Step 3.1 removes the initial change of representative. Coefficient morphisms commute with transport and the formulas, and images of chosen finite lifts are valid lifts for the image cocycle; independence of lifts therefore proves naturality. A commuting scalar action is treated by taking scalar multiples of lifts and using step 3.1.

If $[\alpha]$ comes from a $\mathcal B$ one-cocycle, normalize that cocycle using its own path evaluations. It lifts the normalized image cocycle and has zero coboundary, so its Bockstein is zero. Conversely if $\beta[\alpha]=0$, the lift $b$ from step 2.1 has $\delta b=i(\delta a_1)$ for some $\mathcal A$ one-cochain $a_1$. Then $b-i(a_1)$ is a $\mathcal B$ one-cocycle whose image is $\alpha^0$, so $[\alpha]$ is in the image of $q_*$. This proves exactness at $H^1(M;\mathcal C)$.

Every Bockstein two-cocycle becomes a coboundary in $\mathcal B$ by construction. Conversely let an $\mathcal A$ two-cocycle $a$ become a coboundary $i(a)=\delta b$ for one $\mathcal B$ one-cochain $b$. Its image $\alpha=q(b)$ is a $\mathcal C$ one-cocycle. The $\mathcal B$ zero-cochain $v_x=T_{\gamma_x}^{\mathcal B}b(\gamma_x)$, with $v_o=0$, lifts the normalizing zero-cochain for $\alpha$. Hence $b-\delta v$ lifts $\alpha^0$ and still has coboundary $i(a)$. By step 3.1 it computes the same Bockstein, so $\beta[\alpha]=[a]$. This proves exactness at $H^2(M;\mathcal A)$ and the asserted isomorphism when the two surrounding groups vanish. All lifts used either finitely many generator values, one base-fiber value, or a previously supplied whole cochain. No surjectivity of an infinite product of coefficient quotients was assumed.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.

derivations.claim:
The supplied collars give an open cover of $Y$ by a neighborhood of $W$ and a neighborhood of $X$, retracting onto $W,X$, with intersection retracting onto $A$. In collar coordinates this is obtained by adding a short collar segment across the seam to each side; shrinking its height linearly gives the three retractions. Hence [F1] gives the exact window
$$H_2(A;R)\xrightarrow{(i_W,-i_X)} H_2(W;R)\oplus H_2(X;R)\xrightarrow{j_W+j_X} H_2(Y;R)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_1(A;R) \xrightarrow{(i_W,-i_X)}H_1(W;R)\oplus H_1(X;R).$$
The last arrow is injective, since its $X$ coordinate is injective by hypothesis. Exactness therefore says that $j_W+j_X$ is surjective. This statement is elementwise and does not choose a simultaneous family of preimages.

Write $Q_Y=H_2(Y;R)/\operatorname{im}H_2(D\sqcup B;R)$ and let $\pi$ be its quotient map. Every $x\in H_2(X;R)$ is the image of a class in $H_2(B;R)$, by hypothesis. Its image in $H_2(Y;R)$ therefore lies in the boundary image, so $\pi j_X=0$. For any $y\in H_2(Y;R)$ choose, for this one $y$, a preimage $(w,x)$ under the surjection of step 1.1. Then $\pi(y)=\pi j_W(w)$. Thus $\pi j_W:H_2(W;R)\to Q_Y$ is surjective.

A class from $H_2(D;R)$ maps to zero under $\pi j_W$ because $D$ is a component union of $\partial Y$. A class $a\in H_2(A;R)$ has $j_Wi_W(a)=j_Xi_X(a)$ by the zero composite of the first two Mayer–Vietoris arrows. step 2.1 makes the latter class zero in $Q_Y$. Since $\partial W=A\sqcup D$, every boundary class of $W$ is a sum of these two kinds, so $\pi j_W$ vanishes on the full boundary image. It therefore factors uniquely through the displayed source quotient, and the factored map is surjective by step 2.1. This proves the claimed canonical map, without any assumption on $H_2(A;R)\to H_2(X;R)$.

If the source quotient is a vector space with a finite basis of size $r$, its $r$ images span the target. Finite elimination deletes linearly dependent images until a basis remains, so the target has dimension at most $r$. Only finitely many operations and selections occur. The proof also covers an empty seam or empty outer boundary, zero homology groups and the zero coefficient ring. No step selects representatives for infinitely many classes; surjectivity is used for a single class at a time. Thus the result and the finite-dimensional consequence require no choice principle.

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $M$ a right $R$-module, and $N$ a left $R$-module. Let

$$F:=\mathbb Z^{(M\times N)}$$

be the free $\mathbb Z$-module on the set $M\times N$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]], [[thm-universal-property-of-free-modules]]), and write $e_{(m,n)}$ for its standard basis elements. The additive group of $F$ is abelian. Let $H$ be the subgroup generated ([[def-generated-subgroup]]) by all elements

$$e_{(m+m',n)}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m',n)},$$

$$e_{(m,n+n')}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m,n')},$$

and

$$e_{(mr,n)}-e_{(m,rn)}$$

as $m,m'$ range over $M$, $n,n'$ over $N$, and $r$ over $R$. Since every subgroup of an abelian group is normal, the quotient group $F/H$ is defined ([[def-quotient-group]]). The **tensor product of $M$ and $N$ over $R$** is

$$M\otimes_RN:=F/H.$$

The coset of $e_{(m,n)}$ is the **elementary tensor** $m\otimes n$. Every tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors, because every element of $F$ is a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of basis elements and integer coefficients may be absorbed into either additive variable. The defining relations give

$$(m+m')\otimes n=m\otimes n+m'\otimes n,\qquad m\otimes(n+n')=m\otimes n+m\otimes n',$$

and

$$(mr)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn).$$

In particular $0\otimes n=0=m\otimes0$. No $R$-module structure on $M\otimes_RN$ is part of this arbitrary-ring definition; at this stage it is an abelian group.

Let $C_\bullet$ be a chain complex and let
$$\beta_n:B_n(C)\to Z_n(C)$$
be the canonical morphism supplied by
[[lem-the-boundary-subobject-factors-through-the-cycle-subobject]].

The **$n$th homology object** of $C$ is the cokernel
$$H_n(C):=\operatorname{coker}(\beta_n).$$

Equivalently, one writes
$$H_n(C)=Z_n(C)/B_n(C),$$
with the understanding that this quotient notation abbreviates the cokernel of
the canonical monomorphism from boundaries to cycles.

derivations.claim: For a finite set $S$ of left cosets $Hg$, let $B_S$ be the subgroup of $B$ consisting of sums supported on those cosets. It is a left $A$-submodule, and dropping all coefficients outside those cosets defines a left-$A$ linear projection $B\to B_S$ splitting inclusion. A finite choice of representatives $g_1,\ldots,g_r$ gives the explicit left-$A$ isomorphism $A^r\to B_S$, $(a_j)\mapsto\sum_j a_jg_j$: the supports of distinct summands are disjoint, and translating a supported sum by $g_j^{-1}$ proves surjectivity and uniqueness. Only representatives of this finite set of cosets are used; no global representative system is chosen. Every finite set of elements of $B$ lies in some such $B_S$, by taking the finitely many cosets that meet their supports.

For the fraction clause, send $as^{-1}\in F$, with $a,s\in A$ and $s\ne0$, to the same expression in $K$. If also $as^{-1}=bt^{-1}$ in $F$, choose a nonzero common right multiple $su=tv=w$ in $A$. Multiplying on the right by $w$ gives $au=bv$ in $A$, and the same identity in $K$ proves equality there. Thus the map is well-defined. At a common denominator the addition formula is $(au+bv)w^{-1}$ in both division rings. For a product $as^{-1}bt^{-1}$ with $b\ne0$, choose $bv=su$ nonzero in $A$. Then $s^{-1}b=uv^{-1}$ and the product is $au(tv)^{-1}$ in both rings; the case $b=0$ is immediate. Hence the map preserves multiplication, addition and unit. Its kernel is zero, since $as^{-1}=0$ implies $a=0$ in $K$ and hence in $A$. Uniqueness follows because a ring map extending $A$ must send the inverse of each nonzero $s\in A$ to its inverse in $K$.

Let $f:M'\to M$ be injective. A tensor $z\in M'\otimes_A B$ lies in the image of $M'\otimes_A B_S$ for a finite $S$, by [F1] and step 1.1. If $(f\otimes1)z=0$, apply $1\otimes(B\to B_S)$ to see that its representative $z_S$ maps to zero in $M\otimes_A B_S$. The explicit finite-free coordinates of step 1.1 identify this map with a finite direct sum of copies of $f$, so $z_S=0$ and $z=0$. For arbitrary maps $L\xrightarrow{f}M\xrightarrow{g}N$ exact at $M$, the same finite projection sends a tensor in $\ker(g\otimes1)$ into a finite direct sum of copies of $\ker g=\operatorname{im}f$. Lifting its finitely many coordinates gives a tensor in the image of $f\otimes1$. Conversely that image lies in the kernel since $gf=0$. A surjective map also remains surjective, by lifting the finitely many first coordinates of a tensor expression. Thus extension is exact for arbitrary right modules.

Dropping all coefficients outside $H$ defines an $A$-bimodule map $p:B\to A$ with $p(1)=1$: multiplication by a group element of $H$ on either side preserves both $H$ and its complement. Balancing therefore defines $\rho_M:M\otimes_A B\to M$, $\rho_M(m\otimes b)=mp(b)$. It is right-$A$ linear and satisfies $\rho_M(m\otimes1)=m$. This proves the split unit assertion. If $f\otimes1=0$ for a module homomorphism $f$, then $f(m)=\rho_N((f\otimes1)(m\otimes1))=0$ for each $m$; the functor is faithful. Apply step 2.1 to the exact sequences defining cycles, boundaries and their quotient. It identifies tensor cycles with the kernel of the tensor differential, tensor boundaries with its image, and the tensor quotient with their quotient. The resulting map is $[z]\otimes b\mapsto[z\otimes b]$, proving the natural homology assertion degree by degree. Replacing left cosets by right cosets gives the same finite-coordinate proof for left modules, and the same coefficient projection splits their unit map.

Suppose $q\in F\cap B$. Write $q=as^{-1}$ with $a,s\in A$, $s\ne0$, so $qs=a$. Partition the finite support of $q$ into right cosets $gH$ and choose finitely many representatives, using $1$ for the coset $H$ if it occurs. Thus $q=\sum_j g_jq_j$ with $q_j\in A$. Right multiplication by $s$ preserves each of these coset supports. Since $a$ is supported on $H$, every summand outside that coset satisfies $g_jq_js=0$ as a group-ring element. The absence of zero divisors in $B$ and $s\ne0$ imply $q_j=0$ for each such summand. Therefore $q$ is supported on $H$, which means $q\in A$. The reverse inclusion is given, so $F\cap B=A$. The map of additive quotients $F/A\to K/B$ is well-defined, has kernel $(F\cap B)/A=0$, and respects both $A$ actions because all inclusions are ring maps. Every representative, denominator, lift and coordinate set in this proof belongs to a single finite argument; no simultaneous infinite family is selected. This proves all assertions without a choice principle.

Let $W$ be a compact oriented Hausdorff topological $n$-manifold with boundary $A$ and a supplied boundary collar $c:A\times[0,1)\to W$. Let $\mathcal L$ be a local system of abelian groups. Cap with the integral relative orientation class $z=[W,A]$ gives isomorphisms in every integer degree:
$$H^p(W,A;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(W;\mathcal L),\qquad H^p(W;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(W,A;\mathcal L).$$
The maps commute with every coefficient action commuting with transport, including noncommutative ring actions on the underlying abelian-group systems. No choice principle, smoothness, triangulation or finite CW structure is assumed.

Let $M$ be a compact oriented boundaryless Hausdorff topological $n$-manifold and let $\mathcal L$ be a local system of abelian groups. Cap with its integral orientation class induces isomorphisms
$$H^p(M;\mathcal L)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;\mathcal L)$$
for every integer $p$, without a choice principle. The maps respect any coefficient-ring action commuting with transport, and in particular apply to local systems of modules over a noncommutative ring by forgetting to abelian groups and retaining that action. No smoothness, triangulation or prescribed finite CW structure is assumed.

Let $(M,o)$ be a compact connected based Hausdorff manifold, let $R$ be an involutive unital ring, and supply a rank-one right-$R$ local system $\mathcal R$ with an identification $\mathcal R_o=R$. Assume every based-loop monodromy is left multiplication by a unit $u$ satisfying $\bar u=u^{-1}$. Equip the base fiber with the standard Hermitian form $h_o(a,b)=\bar a b$. Transport extends this to a path-independent parallel Hermitian form $h$ on $\mathcal R$. Put $C_*=C_*(M;\mathcal R)$. For a right $R$-module $P$, write $\overline P$ for its conjugate left module, with $r\cdot\bar p=\overline{p\bar r}$.

The left-$R$ cochain complex $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R)$ is the intrinsic cochain complex of the left-$R$ local system with fiber $R$ and transport $a\mapsto au^{-1}$. Relative to the supplied parallel Hermitian form, that local system is naturally isomorphic to $\overline{\mathcal R}$ by $\bar v\mapsto[w\mapsto h(v,w)]$. The identifications are independent of unitary fiber frames; an arbitrary change of Hermitian structure is not asserted to preserve them. If $M$ is oriented, boundaryless and of dimension $n$, cap duality therefore gives
$$H^p(\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,R))\cong\overline{H_{n-p}(C_*)}.$$
If $R\subseteq K$ is an embedding into an involutive division ring extending the involution, the same conclusion is valid for $K$, with $C_*\otimes_R K$ in the homology target. If $R$ is involution-stable in $K$, the complex $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_*,K/R)$ is the corresponding intrinsic left-$R$ cochain complex with fiber $K/R$ and transport by right multiplication by $u^{-1}$. These identifications require no choice principle and commute with the coefficient maps $R\to K\to K/R$.

Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff manifold, $o\in M$, and $R$ a unital ring. One can construct paths $\gamma_x$ from $o$ to every $x\in M$, with $\gamma_o$ constant, by fixed rules from one finite atlas and finitely many connecting paths. Let $\mathcal R$ be a right-$R$ local system with a supplied identification $\mathcal R_o=R$ and transport given by left multiplication by units, with monodromy image $H\le R^\times$. Its twisted singular complex has an explicit chain decomposition $C_*(M;\mathcal R)=C'_*\oplus Q_*$ after a change of free bases, where $C'_0=R$, $C'_* $ is free, and $Q_*$ is contractible with its only nonzero differential an identity from degree one to degree zero. Moreover
$$\operatorname{im}(d'_1)=\sum_{h\in H}(h-1)R.$$
The decomposition and its dual cochain homotopy equivalences require no choice principle. In particular this image is principal if $H$ is cyclic, if it equals $R$, or if every right ideal of $R$ is principal.

Let $M$ be a compact connected Hausdorff manifold with a basepoint, and let $0\to\mathcal A\xrightarrow{i}\mathcal B\xrightarrow{q}\mathcal C\to0$ be a short exact sequence of local systems of abelian groups on $M$. There is a natural coefficient Bockstein making the sequence
$$H^1(M;\mathcal B)\xrightarrow{q_*}H^1(M;\mathcal C)\xrightarrow{\beta}H^2(M;\mathcal A)\xrightarrow{i_*}H^2(M;\mathcal B)$$
exact at its two middle terms. In particular $\beta$ is an isomorphism if $H^1(M;\mathcal B)=H^2(M;\mathcal B)=0$. No choice principle is assumed. If the local systems and maps have a commuting coefficient-ring action, the sequence and Bockstein respect it.

For $A\subseteq X$ and a local system $\mathcal L$ on $X$, restriction to $A$ gives natural exact sequences

Thus $[\lambda_\eta]=w[\mu_P]$. Equality of $v$ and $w$ is not needed anywhere in this proof. A group G is poly-torsion-free abelian (PTFA) if it admits a finite subnormal series
1=G_0 ◁ G_1 ◁ ⋯ ◁ G_m=G
in which every quotient G_{j+1}/G_j is torsion-free abelian. The trivial group is PTFA, using the length-zero series. The term “subnormal” means each G_j is normal in G_{j+1}; normality in all of G is not required.

Let $k$ be a commutative field and let $H\trianglelefteq G$ be a normal subgroup with torsion-free abelian quotient $G/H$. If $k[H]$ has no zero divisors, then $k[G]$ has no zero divisors. The group extension need not split; neither finite generation of $G/H$ nor an order on all of $G$ is assumed.

A left $R$-module $P$ is **projective** if it has the lifting property for epimorphisms: whenever $q:E\to M$ is a surjective module homomorphism and $f:P\to M$ is a module homomorphism, there exists a module homomorphism $\tilde f:P\to E$ such that $q\circ\tilde f=f$ ([[def-module-homomorphism-kernel-image-and-cokernel]], [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

The lift need not be unique. Projectivity asks for a lift in every such square.

For a unital ring $R$, the **opposite ring** $R^{\mathrm{op}}$ has the same underlying abelian group, identity, and addition as $R$, with multiplication $a\star b:=ba$. Associativity and both distributive laws follow from those of $R$ with the order reversed, and the same element $1$ is a two-sided identity. Thus the displayed operations really form a unital ring, including when $R$ is the zero ring.

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $M$ a right $R$-module, and $N$ a left $R$-module. Let

$$F:=\mathbb Z^{(M\times N)}$$

be the free $\mathbb Z$-module on the set $M\times N$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]], [[thm-universal-property-of-free-modules]]), and write $e_{(m,n)}$ for its standard basis elements. The additive group of $F$ is abelian. Let $H$ be the subgroup generated ([[def-generated-subgroup]]) by all elements

$$e_{(m+m',n)}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m',n)},$$

$$e_{(m,n+n')}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m,n')},$$

and

$$e_{(mr,n)}-e_{(m,rn)}$$

as $m,m'$ range over $M$, $n,n'$ over $N$, and $r$ over $R$. Since every subgroup of an abelian group is normal, the quotient group $F/H$ is defined ([[def-quotient-group]]). The **tensor product of $M$ and $N$ over $R$** is

$$M\otimes_RN:=F/H.$$

The coset of $e_{(m,n)}$ is the **elementary tensor** $m\otimes n$. Every tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors, because every element of $F$ is a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of basis elements and integer coefficients may be absorbed into either additive variable. The defining relations give

$$(m+m')\otimes n=m\otimes n+m'\otimes n,\qquad m\otimes(n+n')=m\otimes n+m\otimes n',$$

and

$$(mr)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn).$$

In particular $0\otimes n=0=m\otimes0$. No $R$-module structure on $M\otimes_RN$ is part of this arbitrary-ring definition; at this stage it is an abelian group.

Let $R$ be a unital ring with $1\ne0$ and no zero divisors. Suppose both Ore conditions hold: any two nonzero elements have a nonzero common right multiple and a nonzero common left multiple. Let $R\subseteq K$ be a unital embedding into a division ring such that every element of $K$ is a right fraction $as^{-1}$ with $a\in R$ and $0\ne s\in R$.

For every right $R$-module $M$, the right $K$-module $M\otimes_RK$ is represented by fractions $[m,s]$ with $m\in M$ and $0\ne s\in R$, corresponding to $m\otimes s^{-1}$. The equality criterion is
$$[m,s]=[n,t]\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{there exist }0\ne u,v\in R\text{ with }su=tv\text{ and }mu=nv.$$
In particular, $[m,s]=0$ if and only if $ma=0$ for some $0\ne a\in R$. Thus the kernel of $M\to M\otimes_RK$, $m\mapsto m\otimes1$, is exactly the set of elements with a nonzero right annihilator, and $M\otimes_RK=0$ if and only if every element of $M$ has a nonzero right annihilator.

The functor $-\otimes_RK$ is exact on arbitrary right $R$-modules, so $K$ is flat as a left $R$-module. For every chain complex $C_\bullet$ of right $R$-modules, the canonical map gives a natural isomorphism
$$H_i(C_\bullet)\otimes_RK\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }H_i(C_\bullet\otimes_RK)$$
for every integer $i$. No finite-generation, finite-presentation or boundedness assumption on the modules or complexes is required.

The corresponding left-module assertions also hold: $K$ is flat as a right $R$-module, $1\otimes m$ is zero in $K\otimes_RM$ precisely when $am=0$ for some $0\ne a\in R$, and $K\otimes_R-$ commutes with the homology of arbitrary left-module chain complexes. All assertions require no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: Call the finite-free property for a group $L$ the implication that a right-$k[L]$ matrix map between finite free modules is injective if its augmentation is injective. If $L$ is torsion-free abelian, [F1] makes $k[L]$ a commutative ring without zero divisors. For an $n$ by $m$ matrix whose augmentation is injective, finite elimination over $k$ gives an $m$ by $m$ minor with nonzero augmented determinant. The determinant of that minor is therefore nonzero in $k[L]$. Multiplying a vector in its kernel by the adjugate shows that this nonzero determinant kills every coordinate. Absence of zero divisors forces all coordinates zero, so the original matrix is injective. This also covers the trivial group and empty matrices.

Suppose $N\trianglelefteq L$, and both $N$ and $L/N$ have the finite-free property. Let $T:k[L]^m\to k[L]^n$ have injective augmentation. Applying the quotient-ring map $k[L]\to k[L/N]$ gives $T_{L/N}$ with the same augmented matrix, hence injective. If $v\in\ker T$, its finitely many coordinates have finite group supports. Choose representatives for the finitely many right-$N$ cosets meeting those supports. In the input, the vectors $e_i g$ for these representatives form a basis of a finite free right-$k[N]$ submodule containing $v$. The finitely many images $T(e_i g)$ are contained in another finite free right-$k[N]$ submodule of the target, obtained by choosing representatives for their finitely many support cosets. Normality ensures that the quotient-ring map sends these coset bases to distinct quotient group elements. Thus the restricted finite $k[N]$ matrix has augmentation equal to the $k$-linear restriction of $T_{L/N}$ to the corresponding finite span of quotient basis elements. That restriction is injective, so the finite-free property of $N$ makes the restricted matrix injective. Consequently $v=0$. Only finite sets of coset representatives were selected; no global transversal or splitting was used.

Induct up a finite PTFA subnormal series. The trivial subgroup has the property by step 1.1; at each step the preceding subgroup is normal in the next and the quotient is torsion-free abelian. Steps 1.1 and 1.2 therefore prove the finite-free property for that next subgroup. This uses only the successive normalities given in [F1], not normality of the whole series in $G$. After finitely many steps, $G$ has the finite-free property.

The same detection property holds for a map between free $k[G]$ modules of arbitrary ranks. Indeed a proposed nonzero kernel vector uses finitely many input basis elements; their images use finitely many target basis elements. Restricting to those finite free submodules preserves injectivity of the augmented map, because their inclusions into the larger free modules are split coordinate inclusions and remain so after augmentation. The finite-free property of step 2.1 makes the restriction injective, contradicting the proposed vector. No arbitrary free module is being asserted projective in the absence of choice.

Put $A=k[G]$ and let $f:P\to Q$ be as in the Statement. The canonical free module $F_P=A^{(P)}$ on the underlying set of $P$ has a surjection $\pi_P:F_P\to P$ sending $e_p$ to $p$. Projectivity gives one section $s_P$, and similarly gives $\pi_Q:F_Q\to Q$ and a section $s_Q$. Set $e=s_P\pi_P$, so $e^2=e$. Define a map between actual free modules $$g:F_P\longrightarrow F_Q\oplus F_P,\qquad g(x)=(s_Qf\pi_Px,(1-e)x).$$ If an augmented vector $\xi$ lies in $\ker(g\otimes k)$, its second coordinate says $\xi=(s_P\otimes k)(\pi_P\otimes k)\xi$. Since $s_Q\otimes k$ has left inverse $\pi_Q\otimes k$, its first coordinate implies $(f\otimes k)(\pi_P\otimes k)\xi=0$. The assumed injectivity yields $(\pi_P\otimes k)\xi=0$, and hence $\xi=0$. Thus $g\otimes k$ is injective, so $g$ is injective by step 3.1. For $p\in\ker f$, $g(s_Pp)=0$; therefore $s_Pp=0$ and $p=0$. The two sections are supplied by the two individual projectivity assertions, not by a simultaneous lift selection. This proves the full right-projective assertion.

Inversion $g\mapsto g^{-1}$ and the identity on $k$ give an anti-isomorphism of $k[G]$ with itself that preserves augmentation. It converts left modules into right modules, preserves the individual lifting property, and converts the augmented injectivity question to the one proved in step 4.1. Hence the left-projective assertion holds too. This is an explicit opposite-ring change and chooses neither bases nor representatives.

Let $r$ be the rank of the finite augmented matrix $\varepsilon T$. Choose $r$ input columns and $r$ output rows giving an invertible augmented square minor; this is finite elimination over $k$. Its unaugmented square matrix is injective over $k[G]$ by step 2.1, and remains injective over $K$ by [F3]. Finite-dimensional division-ring elimination therefore gives it rank $r$ over $K$. It is a row projection of the corresponding $r$ columns of $T\otimes K$, so those columns are independent and the full matrix has rank at least $r$. The case $r=0$ is automatic. All eliminations, supports, sections and coset choices in the proof are finite or individually supplied; no basis of a projective module or infinite family of coset representatives was selected. Thus both detection and the stated rank comparison hold without a choice axiom.

Let $k$ be a commutative field and $G$ a PTFA group. For every homomorphism $f:P\to Q$ between projective right-$k[G]$ modules, if
$$f\otimes1:P\otimes_{k[G]}k\longrightarrow Q\otimes_{k[G]}k$$
is injective under the augmentation $k[G]\to k$, then $f$ is injective. Projective means the lifting property for surjections, applied to right modules; it does not mean a supplied free basis. Thus this is the right-module defining property of Strebel's class $D(k)$. The left-module version holds too.

Moreover, if $k[G]\subseteq K$ is a supplied division ring of Ore fractions, every finite matrix $T$ over $k[G]$ satisfies
$$\operatorname{rank}_K(T\otimes K)\ge\operatorname{rank}_k(\varepsilon T).$$
Both assertions require no choice axiom. The group need not be finitely generated, its series need not be normal in all of $G$, and its successive extensions need not split.

A left $R$-module $P$ is **projective** if it has the lifting property for epimorphisms: whenever $q:E\to M$ is a surjective module homomorphism and $f:P\to M$ is a module homomorphism, there exists a module homomorphism $\tilde f:P\to E$ such that $q\circ\tilde f=f$ ([[def-module-homomorphism-kernel-image-and-cokernel]], [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

The lift need not be unique. Projectivity asks for a lift in every such square.

For a unital ring $R$, the **opposite ring** $R^{\mathrm{op}}$ has the same underlying abelian group, identity, and addition as $R$, with multiplication $a\star b:=ba$. Associativity and both distributive laws follow from those of $R$ with the order reversed, and the same element $1$ is a two-sided identity. Thus the displayed operations really form a unital ring, including when $R$ is the zero ring.

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $M$ a right $R$-module, and $N$ a left $R$-module. Let

$$F:=\mathbb Z^{(M\times N)}$$

be the free $\mathbb Z$-module on the set $M\times N$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]], [[thm-universal-property-of-free-modules]]), and write $e_{(m,n)}$ for its standard basis elements. The additive group of $F$ is abelian. Let $H$ be the subgroup generated ([[def-generated-subgroup]]) by all elements

$$e_{(m+m',n)}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m',n)},$$

$$e_{(m,n+n')}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m,n')},$$

and

$$e_{(mr,n)}-e_{(m,rn)}$$

as $m,m'$ range over $M$, $n,n'$ over $N$, and $r$ over $R$. Since every subgroup of an abelian group is normal, the quotient group $F/H$ is defined ([[def-quotient-group]]). The **tensor product of $M$ and $N$ over $R$** is

$$M\otimes_RN:=F/H.$$

The coset of $e_{(m,n)}$ is the **elementary tensor** $m\otimes n$. Every tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors, because every element of $F$ is a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of basis elements and integer coefficients may be absorbed into either additive variable. The defining relations give

$$(m+m')\otimes n=m\otimes n+m'\otimes n,\qquad m\otimes(n+n')=m\otimes n+m\otimes n',$$

and

$$(mr)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn).$$

In particular $0\otimes n=0=m\otimes0$. No $R$-module structure on $M\otimes_RN$ is part of this arbitrary-ring definition; at this stage it is an abelian group.

derivations.claim: Choose a finite generating list for $P$, giving a surjection $\pi:A^n\to P$. Projectivity gives one section $s:P\to A^n$. The matrix $E=s\pi$ is idempotent, and after either base change $P$ identifies with the image of that idempotent. Put $r=\operatorname{rank}_k E_k$. By [F1], $\operatorname{rank}_K E_K\ge r$ and $\operatorname{rank}_K(1-E)_K\ge n-r$. Idempotency gives the actual complementary decomposition $K^n=\operatorname{im}E_K\oplus\operatorname{im}(1-E)_K$: every vector is the sum of its two displayed images, and their intersection is zero after applying $E_K$. Their dimensions therefore add to $n$, forcing equality in both inequalities. Hence $\dim_K P_K=r=\dim_k P_k$. Only one finite generating list and one projectivity section were used.

Take finite split surjections $\pi_P:A^m\to P$ and $\pi_Q:A^n\to Q$, with sections $s_P,s_Q$. The finite matrix $T=s_Qf\pi_P$ has, after either base change, the same image dimension as $f$: the map $\pi_P$ remains surjective and $s_Q$ remains injective by their split identities. Applying [F1] to $T$ yields $\dim_K\operatorname{im}f_K\ge\dim_k\operatorname{im}f_k$. This argument does not treat $P$ or $Q$ as free.

For a bounded complex after either base change all chain groups are finite-dimensional. If $d_i:P_i\to P_{i-1}$ is its differential, finite-dimensional rank-nullity and cycles modulo boundaries give $$\dim (P_i)_*=\operatorname{rank}(d_i)_*+\dim H_i(P_*)+\operatorname{rank}(d_{i+1})_*,$$ where $*$ is $k$ or $K$. Summing with signs over the finite range cancels every differential rank, so the alternating homology dimension equals the alternating chain dimension. The latter sums are equal under the two base changes by step 1.1. This proves the asserted Euler equality, with no boundedness or generation conclusion inferred for an unrelated singular complex.

In the nonnegative case, $d_0=0$. Write $n_i=\dim_k(P_i)_k=\dim_K(P_i)_K$. The degree-zero hypotheses give $\operatorname{rank}(d_1)_k=n_0-1$ and $\operatorname{rank}(d_1)_K=n_0$. Step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{rank}(d_2)_K\ge\operatorname{rank}(d_2)_k$. Therefore $$\dim_K H_1(P_K)=n_1-n_0-\operatorname{rank}(d_2)_K\le n_1-n_0-\operatorname{rank}(d_2)_k=\dim_k H_1(P_k)-1.$$ Every section and generating set needed for the bounded complex belongs to one finite list; finite elimination over $k$ and $K$ requires no choice axiom. This proves all assertions in their stated projective scope.
